Hypothesis: Neutron stars born in supernova remnants (SNRs) and observed as SGR-like bursting sources admit a jointly constrained evolutionary trajectory in which (i) kinematics (proper motion and/or IPN burst-triangulation localization) and a marginalised SNR-evolution age model constrain the birth site, transverse velocity, and true age, while (ii) the observed thermal emission is governed by magneto-thermal coupling (anisotropic conduction + field-decay-driven Joule heating) whose time-curvature in luminosity/temperature cannot be mimicked by arbitrary age shifts once kinematics and SNR physics are enforced. Mechanism for overcoming reviewer-identified limitations: (A) Identifiability is obtained by explicitly restricting the thermal-emission forward model to combinations of (M,R,B-field evolution, envelope composition) that reproduce not only the phase-averaged spectrum but also the age–temperature locus implied by the kinematic/SNR posterior, and by using observables that respond differently to distance/NH vs redshifted radius (e.g., multi-epoch flux evolution where available, pulsed fraction constraints when present, and the fact that magneto-thermal models impose a constrained relation between surface anisotropy and integrated luminosity). We will quantify the remaining (M,R) information content with simulation-based forecasts (Fisher + SBC-calibrated posterior contraction) under realistic systematics (distance, NH, atmosphere composition, beaming). (B) SNR ages will not be treated as point estimates (e.g., Sedov-only), but as a fully marginalised dynamical submodel over explosion energy and ambient density (optionally informed by measured shock temperature/velocity), including selection effects in SNR detectability and counterpart follow-up; this prevents biased ages feeding into B-decay inferences. (C) IPN localization will be treated with a tiered likelihood strategy: when timing/ephemeris covariance products exist we reconstruct annulus likelihoods from time-delay residuals; otherwise we use a principled fallback that still improves on rectangle/ellipse overlap by converting published annulus parameters and widths into a normalized sky probability density and integrating it over the SNR-informed birth-site/trajectory distribution. (D) Magneto-thermal emulation will be governed by a training-set design spanning Hall+Ohmic regimes, envelope compositions, and superfluid assumptions; we will enforce calibration with posterior predictive checks and simulation-based calibration to prevent surrogate-driven overconfidence in (M,R)/EoS. Under these constraints, the joint model is expected to (1) reduce false SNR associations allowed by large IPN error regions, and (2) yield quantified, not overstated, incremental constraints on (M,R) and EoS hyperparameters relative to standard spectral-only analyses, with the improvement explicitly forecast as a function of distance/NH/systematic floors.
Plan:
Step 0 — Scope, deliverables, and decision gates
0.1 Define two deliverables with quantitative success criteria:
  (D1) Association: Bayes factor (source-in-SNR vs chance alignment) and posterior on age and v⊥ for each candidate; success = demonstrable reduction in false-association rate in synthetic injections at fixed completeness.
  (D2) EoS: posterior contraction on (M,R) or EoS hyperparameters relative to a baseline (standard phase-averaged thermal spectral fit with weak priors); success = forecasted and validated contraction factor under specified systematic assumptions, with SBC showing calibrated posteriors.
0.2 Implement decision gates to prevent over-claiming EoS constraints:
  Gate G1: If identifiability forecasts show <10–20% contraction in R for realistic distance/NH/atmosphere uncertainty in a given target, we will report association + B-decay constraints but not claim meaningful EoS improvement for that target.

Step 1 — Target assembly tied to the concept chain (IPN → SNR → thermal emission)
1.1 Build a sample of SGR-like bursting sources localized by IPN (Ulysses + KONUS-WIND; add BATSE where available) with:
  - Published annulus parameters (center vector, annulus radius, half-width / 1σ timing uncertainty equivalent) and intersection polygons (when provided).
  - Candidate X-ray counterparts with reported thermal components (blackbody or atmosphere) and measured NH constraints.
  - Candidate SNRs with angular size, morphology classification (shell/PWN/mixed), distance estimates (with priors), and any shock diagnostics (kT_shock, v_s, proper motions of filaments) when available.
1.2 Add calibration/benchmark systems:
  - Kinematics benchmark: pulsar/SNR with measured proper motion and offset-based age consistency checks (e.g., PSR B1951+32/CTB 80 archetype for μ ↔ v⊥ mapping).
  - Thermal benchmark: high-B thermally emitting neutron stars (RRAT-like systems) to validate magneto-thermal predictions for kT ~ 0.1 keV and ages ~10^5 yr.

Step 2 — IPN likelihood inputs: concrete data products + fallbacks
2.1 Tier-1 (preferred) IPN likelihood reconstruction (requires timing residual covariances):
  - Inputs: published burst arrival-time differences Δt_ij between spacecraft i,j (or equivalent annulus radius), spacecraft ephemerides (position vectors at burst epoch), and quoted timing uncertainties (including systematics).
  - Likelihood: for each burst b and spacecraft pair (i,j), compute predicted Δt_ij(α,δ) = (r_i − r_j)·n(α,δ)/c and use a Gaussian or Student-t residual model with covariance Σ_b (Student-t to robustify unmodeled clock systematics).
  - Multiply over bursts and pairs: L_IPN(α,δ) ∝ ∏_b ∏_(i,j) p(Δt_ij,b | α,δ, Σ_b).
  - Output: normalized sky pdf on a HEALPix grid at resolution set by annulus width.
2.2 Tier-2 (publication-level) reconstruction when full timing is unavailable:
  - Inputs: published annulus center great-circle parameters + quoted half-widths; published intersection box/polygon vertices if available.
  - Construct an annulus-band likelihood per annulus k: p_k(α,δ) ∝ exp[−(Δθ_k(α,δ))^2/(2σ_k^2)] where Δθ_k is angular distance to the annulus midline; truncate outside reported band if only a hard width is available.
  - For multiple annuli, multiply and renormalize; if a box/polygon is provided, use it as a hard mask multiplied by the smooth band product.
  - Demonstrable advantage vs ellipse/rectangle: we retain curved-sky geometry and correctly weight corners/edges rather than uniform probability inside a box.
2.3 Validation of IPN likelihood layer:
  - Reproduce published error-box areas and verify that the maximum-likelihood region coincides with reported intersection regions.
  - Sensitivity analysis: vary σ_k within quoted systematic ranges to see impact on association Bayes factors.

Step 3 — SNR evolution and age: explicit marginalised submodel + selection effects
3.1 Dynamical age model with marginalisation:
  - Model class chosen per SNR type:
    (a) Shell-dominated: Sedov-Taylor with parameters {E_51, n0, t, d, ξ_morph}.
    (b) If radiative/transition indicators exist: include a pressure-driven snowplow extension with an additional transition time parameter.
    (c) PWN-in-SNR cases: include a coupled PWN expansion component with pulsar spindown power prior (broad) and pressure balance.
  - Observables used when available:
    - Angular radius θ_snr and distance d → physical radius R_snr.
    - Shock temperature kT_s or shock velocity v_s (from X-ray spectroscopy or optical proper motions) to constrain v_s(t) and thus t.
  - Priors:
    - Explosion energy: log-uniform or weakly informative around 10^51 erg (e.g., log10 E in [50.5, 51.5]).
    - Ambient density: log-uniform over plausible ISM ranges with SNR-dependent bounds.
    - Morphology nuisance ξ_morph to inflate model discrepancy (accounts for asymmetry/clumping) via a multiplicative radius error term.
  - Output: p(t, d, R_snr | data) with E and n0 marginalised.
3.2 Association selection function:
  - Model probability of including an SNR in the candidate set as S(d, NH, surface brightness Σ, angular size), with hyperparameters learned from an external SNR catalogue (e.g., MOST-like completeness curves) or bracketed with sensitivity analyses.
  - Incorporate into hierarchical inference so chance association odds are not biased by detectability.

Step 4 — Kinematics module (proper motion/IPN + birth-site prior)
4.1 Birth-site prior inside SNR:
  - Mixture prior reflecting uncertain explosion site: p(r0 | SNR) = w_shell Uniform(volume) + (1−w_shell) P(morphology-weighted), where morphology-weighted concentrates near geometric center but allows offsets along observed brightness gradients.
4.2 Forward model:
  - Given {t, d, r0} and current position r, compute μ = |r−r0|/t and v⊥ = |r−r0| d / t.
  - Natal-kick prior: broad but explicit (e.g., mixture of Maxwellians) and allow magnetar-like tails; hyperparameters can be shared across the sample.
4.3 Likelihood terms:
  - IPN: integrate L_IPN(α,δ) against the (counterpart position ⊗ astrometric uncertainty) distribution.
  - Proper motion: Gaussian likelihood for μ when measured.
  - Containment/consistency: require trajectory not to imply unphysical exit far beyond SNR bounds given age, with slack absorbed by ξ_morph.

Step 5 — Magneto-thermal emission module with governed complexity
5.1 Physics parameterisation (restricted to identifiable degrees of freedom):
  - Core thermal evolution parameters: {B0_dip, B0_tor/B0_tot (toroidal fraction), τ_Ohm, τ_Hall, Q_imp (crust impurity), envelope composition class (light vs heavy), superfluid gap model index (discrete set)}.
  - Geometry: enforce dipole-dominated surface field plus toroidal component; represent surface temperature T(θ) with low-order spherical harmonics consistent with dipole symmetry to avoid unconstrained high-l modes.
  - Microphysics envelopes: include both light-element and heavy-element envelopes because they dominate surface T–core T mapping systematics.
5.2 Forward spectral model:
  - For each parameter draw, compute predicted T_eff(θ,t) and redshifted emission; generate phase-averaged spectrum with viewing-angle marginalisation.
  - Atmosphere systematics handling:
    - Use a model set: blackbody, H atmosphere, heavy-element atmosphere (where applicable), and magnetized atmosphere approximations parameterized by B and composition.
    - Treat atmosphere choice as a discrete model index with Bayesian model averaging rather than a single assumed model.
  - Absorption: NH with priors from X-ray fits and (where possible) external constraints; propagate explicitly.
  - Distance: infer jointly with SNR distance prior; do not fix.
5.3 Emulator design (surrogate of 2D magneto-thermal evolution):
  - Training grid spans Hall+Ohmic regimes by covering (B0, τ_Hall, τ_Ohm) ranges appropriate for B > 10^13 G, and ages 10^3–10^6 yr.
  - Include envelope composition (binary) and multiple superfluid prescriptions as categorical inputs.
  - Output targets: physically constrained latent quantities {Lν(t), Lγ(t), H_J(t), plus low-order coefficients of T(θ,t)}; enforce global energy equation dE_th/dt = −Lν − Lγ + H_J in the surrogate either by (i) predicting the terms and numerically integrating E_th, or (ii) adding a hard constraint loss during training.
  - Out-of-distribution (OOD) checks: compute emulator uncertainty and reject/temper samples outside convex hull of training data (e.g., via Mahalanobis distance in input space and predictive variance thresholds).

Step 6 — Identifiability & forecasting (mandatory quantitative section)
6.1 Baseline vs joint-model forecasts:
  - Define baseline analysis: phase-averaged spectral fit with free (kT, norm), NH, distance prior; infer an apparent radius R_app with broad priors; no kinematic/SNR coupling; no magneto-thermal time constraint.
  - Define joint analysis: full model with kinematic age posterior + magneto-thermal evolution + atmosphere model averaging.
6.2 Simulation-based forecast protocol (per target archetype):
  - Generate synthetic datasets under realistic conditions:
    - Distance uncertainty: e.g., 20–50% (SNR distance priors).
    - NH uncertainty: from spectral covariance + systematic floor (e.g., ±(10–30)%).
    - Atmosphere mismatch: generate with one atmosphere, fit with model-averaging set.
    - Beaming/anisotropy: draw from viewing geometry distribution and magneto-thermal T(θ) outputs.
  - Observables: phase-averaged spectra (and pulsed fraction if available); optionally multi-epoch flux (if archival epochs exist).
  - Compute posterior contraction metrics: expected reduction in σ(R) and σ(M) (or in EoS hyperparameters) relative to baseline; report as a function of data quality (counts), distance/NH priors, and presence/absence of pulsed fraction.
6.3 Fisher information cross-check:
  - Compute approximate Fisher matrices for reduced parameter sets to diagnose which parameters drive degeneracy (e.g., (R∞/d)^2 vs NH vs atmosphere choice) and identify where kinematic age breaks degeneracy via cooling-curve slope/curvature.
6.4 Deliverable: an explicit table/plot in the proposal output package (not just narrative) showing achievable ΔR (km) or fractional improvement under stated uncertainties; use this to bound EoS claims.

Step 7 — Joint inference and model comparison
7.1 Hierarchical Bayesian model:
  - Global hyperparameters: natal-kick distribution parameters; SNR selection-function parameters; magneto-thermal population priors.
  - Per-source parameters: {association flag, r0, t, d, v⊥, μ, NH, atmosphere model index, (M,R) or EoS hyperparameters, magneto-thermal parameters}.
7.2 Inference engine:
  - Use nested sampling for multimodal posteriors (association on/off; discrete atmosphere models) or HMC with marginalization over discrete indices via enumeration.
  - Implement IPN likelihood integrals on HEALPix with caching to make evidence computations tractable.
7.3 Model comparisons (Bayes factors):
  - Association: source-in-SNR vs chance alignment under selection function.
  - Cooling: magneto-thermal (with B-decay heating) vs minimal cooling.
  - EoS families: compare EoS hyperparameterizations subject to causality (c_s ≤ c) and stability; report only if identifiability gate G1 is met.

Step 8 — Emulator governance, calibration, and robustness
8.1 Training-set design review:
  - Document parameter ranges, categorical physics choices, and age grid; ensure coverage of Hall-dominated early evolution and Ohmic-dominated late evolution.
8.2 Simulation-based calibration (SBC):
  - Draw parameters from priors, simulate spectra + IPN localizations + SNR observables, run full inference, and verify rank statistics are uniform for key parameters (age, B0, R).
  - If miscalibration appears, inflate likelihood/systematic terms or adjust emulator uncertainty model.
8.3 Posterior predictive checks:
  - Compare predicted spectra, fluxes, and (if used) pulsed fractions against data; check residuals for structure indicating atmosphere/systematics mismatch.
8.4 Sensitivity analyses:
  - Vary SNR selection function; alternative SNR evolution models; alternative NH priors; alternative atmosphere sets; examine stability of association odds and (M,R) posteriors.

Step 9 — Reporting policy to avoid overstated EoS payoff
9.1 Report (M,R)/EoS constraints only with:
  - Identifiability forecast showing expected improvement above baseline;
  - SBC-calibrated posteriors;
  - Explicit accounting of atmosphere/distance/NH systematics via model averaging and nuisance priors.
9.2 Otherwise report: association probabilities, kinematics (v⊥), age posteriors, and B-decay/Joule-heating constraints as primary outcomes.
Feasibility:
Addresses (1) Data identifiability: We do not assume phase-averaged spectra alone determine emitting area. Instead we (i) quantify expected posterior contraction on (M,R) via simulation-based forecasts under realistic distance/NH/atmosphere/beaming uncertainties, (ii) restrict magneto-thermal degrees of freedom to a governed, low-order anisotropy representation and a small set of physically motivated parameters, and (iii) use Bayesian model averaging over atmosphere compositions to prevent spurious tightening. We impose explicit decision gates (G1) so EoS claims are made only where the forecasts and calibration indicate real information gain.

Addresses (2) SNR age modeling: We replace point-estimate Sedov ages with a marginalised SNR dynamical model over explosion energy and ambient density, optionally constrained by shock velocity/temperature when available, and include a morphology discrepancy parameter to absorb asymmetries. We further incorporate an SNR selection function to prevent biased association odds and biased age posteriors driven by detectability.

Addresses (3) IPN likelihood reconstruction feasibility: We specify a tiered input plan. Tier-1 reconstructs likelihoods from time-delay residual models when timing/covariance/ephemeris products exist; Tier-2 uses published annulus parameters (radius/width) to build a normalized curved-sky probability density, preserving non-Gaussian geometry and enabling correct integration with SNR-informed birth-site priors. Even Tier-2 improves on rectangle/ellipse overlap because probability mass is correctly distributed along annulus intersections rather than assumed uniform.

Addresses (4) Emulator validity and overconfidence: The surrogate is governed by (i) a training design spanning Hall + Ohmic regimes, envelope composition, and discrete superfluid prescriptions; (ii) explicit OOD detection/tempering; and (iii) calibration via simulation-based calibration and posterior predictive checks. This directly targets the risk of artificially overconfident posteriors and ensures the emulator does not exceed its validated domain.

Scientific grounding in the provided literature chain: Proper motion ↔ transverse velocity mapping and offset-based age inference are validated in pulsar/SNR systems (Asset 1). IPN triangulation provides geometrical localizations with potentially large but structured uncertainties that must be treated probabilistically (Asset 2). Thermal emission from cooling neutron stars is observed in high-B objects and motivates magneto-thermal modeling (Asset 3), while strong magnetic fields modify cooling via anisotropic conductivity and Joule heating from field decay on ~10^6 yr timescales (Asset 4). The proposal’s novelty is not any single element but the physically constrained coupling—kinematics and marginalised SNR ages prevent magneto-thermal parameters from absorbing incorrect ages/distances, while governed magneto-thermal evolution provides a time-structured prior on thermal observables. The expected outcome is a robust reduction in false SNR associations and a calibrated, quantitatively bounded improvement in (M,R)/EoS inference where data quality permits.
Critique: This is an unusually detailed and methodologically mature proposal. The engineering plan is concrete, modular, and realistically executable with existing data products, particularly the tiered IPN likelihood strategy and the marginalised SNR age submodel. Logical consistency is strong: the central identifiability argument—that kinematic/SNR-constrained ages prevent magneto-thermal models from absorbing arbitrary age shifts—is physically sound and well defended with decision gates and forecasting. Evidence grounding is solid; all components are standard within high-energy astrophysics and neutron-star physics, and their coupling is justified rather than ad hoc. Minor deductions arise from residual ambition risk: the emulator governance and hierarchical model complexity may strain practical inference for small samples, and the anticipated EoS gains, while carefully bounded, are likely to be marginal except in best-case systems. Nonetheless, the proposal is self-aware of these limits and explicitly guards against over-claiming.

Hypothesis: A measurable gamma-ray counterpart to a subset of large neutron-star glitches is produced when rapid, avalanche-like unpinning of core/inner-crust superfluid vortices triggers a transient increase in mutual-friction dissipation and magnetospheric current injection; the dissipated mechanical energy heats a thin outer layer and drives pair cascades whose prompt spectrum and fluence scale with the glitch-released angular momentum and the core superfluid coupling timescale. We will test this by a methodological adaptation: a physics-constrained Bayesian state-space inversion that couples pulsar timing (spin frequency and spin-down changes) to a superfluid vortex-dynamics forward model and to a magnetospheric radiative transfer surrogate, with hard constraints from angular-momentum conservation, superfluid hydrodynamics, and causality/EOS bounds enforced directly in the inference (constraint-augmented likelihood and TOV/causality-prior). Mechanistically, enforcing continuity of vorticity and density-dependent pinning in spherical geometry makes the inferred glitch energy budget and dissipation profile identifiable, enabling a falsifiable prediction for contemporaneous gamma-ray fluence and temporal morphology.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Build a joint dataset of (i) high-cadence gamma-ray pulsar timing (Fermi-LAT and, where available, radio/X-ray timing) containing detected glitches/anti-glitches with uncertainties in Δν, Δνdot, recovery components; (ii) time-tagged gamma-ray photon data around each event to construct phase-resolved light curves and transient searches; (iii) auxiliary constraints (distance, B-field estimate, age, thermal X-ray constraints when available).
1.2 Define event windows and control windows for each glitch to quantify gamma-ray excess/changes in pulsed fraction/spectral hardness while controlling for LAT exposure systematics.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Forward model (superfluid + vortex dynamics): implement a two-component (crust + superfluid) angular-momentum exchange model with spherical-geometry vortex continuity across crust/core, density-dependent pinning forces, and creep/mutual-friction prescriptions; include an unpinning avalanche trigger parameterization that releases a fraction of pinned vorticity on a short timescale, producing ΔΩ and recovery.
2.2 Mechanistic energy channel: compute dissipation rate from mutual friction and differential rotation during the post-trigger coupling; map dissipation to a surface heating/current-injection driver via an electrodynamic coupling term (parameterized but energy-conserving), yielding a predicted gamma-ray luminosity time profile and spectral pivot (e.g., change in cutoff energy) through a magnetospheric emission surrogate.
2.3 Methodological adaptation (constraint-respecting inference): construct a Bayesian state-space model with latent states {Ωc(t), Ωs(t), lag(t), pinned-vorticity reservoir(t)} and observation models for timing and gamma-ray data. Enforce: (i) exact angular-momentum conservation across components during the glitch impulse; (ii) positivity and microphysical bounds on pinning force and mutual-friction coefficients; (iii) EOS/TOV-causality prior that restricts allowable density profiles and superfluid moment of inertia fractions (e.g., speed of sound < c, maximum mass constraints) thereby bounding the reservoir size and coupling timescales.
2.4 Implement inference with particle MCMC / SMC that can handle impulsive events and non-Gaussian posteriors; embed constraints as hard rejections or differentiable barrier terms in the log-posterior to prevent unphysical solutions.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Posterior predictive checks: verify that the inferred vortex unpinning and creep parameters reproduce both the instantaneous Δν, Δνdot and the multi-timescale recovery for each glitch.
3.2 Gamma-ray counterpart test: quantify Bayes factors comparing models with and without the dissipation-to-gamma coupling, using phase-resolved likelihoods (pulsed component) to distinguish magnetospheric changes from background.
3.3 Cross-event scaling laws: test predicted relations such as gamma-ray fluence ∝ ΔL_gl (or ∝ I_sf·ΔΩ) modulated by coupling time τ_mf; verify whether the largest glitches in gamma-ray-only pulsars preferentially show detectable hardening or transient pulsed-flux enhancements.
3.4 Falsification: demonstrate that any inferred gamma-ray energy never exceeds the available mechanical reservoir from the constrained superfluid model; if observed gamma-ray energetics exceed this bound, rule out the vortex-dissipation mechanism for those events and favor external/impact scenarios.
3.5 EOS impact: propagate EOS-prior variations to predicted counterpart rates, producing constraints on core superfluid moment of inertia fraction and mutual-friction strength consistent with multi-messenger bounds.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Glitches are naturally explained by superfluid vortex unpinning and subsequent angular-momentum transfer; realistic spherical-geometry pinning/creep models with density-dependent forces reproduce Vela-like glitch amplitudes and recoveries, implying an available dissipation channel during recoupling. High-energy emission changes are expected if magnetospheric currents respond to rapid changes in rotation or surface heating, making a gamma-ray counterpart physically plausible but energetically bounded.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): State-space inference is established for timing noise/glitch recovery, but standard approaches treat microphysics and EOS weakly or as post-processing. The adaptation hard-wires conservation laws, vorticity continuity, and EOS/causality bounds into the inference so that inferred energy budgets and coupling timescales are physically valid, directly enabling a mechanistic link from vortex dynamics to gamma-ray emission.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to unconstrained regressions or purely phenomenological glitch fits, the constraint-augmented Bayesian inversion yields identifiable, EOS-aware posteriors for the superfluid reservoir and dissipation history, producing falsifiable predictions for gamma-ray fluence/spectral evolution and event rates. It also cleanly separates internal (vortex) mechanisms from external (impact/anti-glitch) scenarios by enforcing strict energy and angular-momentum accounting, improving interpretability and reducing false associations in counterpart searches.
Critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and internally consistent proposal that clearly reflects deep familiarity with neutron-star glitch microphysics, modern pulsar timing analysis, and Bayesian inference under physical constraints. The strongest aspect is the explicit enforcement of conservation laws and EOS/causality bounds within the inference itself, which directly addresses a real identifiability bottleneck in glitch energetics. The logical chain from vortex unpinning to dissipation to a gamma-ray observable is plausible and carefully energy-bounded, avoiding a common pitfall in multi-messenger counterpart claims. Minor weaknesses arise from the magnetospheric emission surrogate, which remains relatively phenomenological compared to the rigor of the superfluid modeling, and from feasibility risk: LAT photon statistics around individual glitches may limit the power of the Bayes-factor tests except for a very small subset of events. These are executional rather than conceptual deficiencies.

Hypothesis: A joint gravitational-wave + electromagnetic hierarchical inference that enforces exact relativistic structure constraints will (i) reduce degeneracies between component masses/spins and tidal effects that currently blur the neutron-star/black-hole mass gap, and (ii) yield a less biased standard-siren Hubble parameter measurement from binary-neutron-star and neutron-star–black-hole events. Methodological adaptation: replace the standard unconstrained event-level parameter estimation with a physics-constrained, trans-dimensional Bayesian model in which (a) neutron-star tidal deformabilities are not free waveform parameters but are generated by an equation-of-state latent function passed through a TOV solver with strict causality/stability bounds, and (b) the compact-object type (NS vs BH) is a discrete latent variable coupled to the mass-gap prior and to an EM-informed ejecta/kilonova likelihood. Mechanism: enforcing the TOV mapping (EoS → {M,R,Λ}) and relativistic causality (cs<=c) collapses the physically allowed Λ(m) manifold, breaking the mass–spin–tidal degeneracy in inspiral waveforms; simultaneously, coupling the discrete type variable to kilonova brightness/ejecta predictions suppresses posterior support for mass-gap solutions that would be inconsistent with observed (or non-detected) EM counterparts, thereby sharpening classification and improving distance–inclination inference that propagates to H0.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
- Curate LIGO-Virgo (Virgo Collaboration-inclusive) BNS/NSBH candidate set with strain data and calibration uncertainty models; include sub-threshold candidates with per-event P_astro weights to control purity rather than fixed FAR cuts.
- Assemble EM follow-up products where available (host redshift, sky map overlap, kilonova photometry/upper limits) and standardized selection functions for EM detectability.
- Define a flexible EoS latent parameterization (e.g., spectral or piecewise-polytrope) with priors enforcing thermodynamic stability (dP/dε>0) and causality (cs^2=dP/dε<=1) and matching to known crust models at low density.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
- Implement a constrained generative EoS→TOV→{M(R),Λ(m)} module embedded inside the Bayesian sampler: each proposed EoS draws a whole Λ(m) curve and maximum mass M_TOV; proposals violating causality, stability, or observed 2-solar-mass constraints are rejected (hard constraints) or down-weighted (soft barrier) to ensure physical validity.
- Build a trans-dimensional compact-object classifier: for each event, include a discrete latent variable z∈{BNS,NSBH,BBH} with mixture weights informed by a mass-gap population hyperprior; for NS components, tidal terms are set by Λ(m) from the EoS module; for BH components, Λ=0 and spin priors include precession.
- Couple GW likelihood to an EM-informed likelihood: use semi-analytic ejecta fits conditioned on (masses, spins, EoS) to predict kilonova luminosity distributions; incorporate detections as photometric likelihoods and non-detections as censoring/upper-limit likelihoods to penalize configurations that would overproduce observable kilonovae.
- Perform hierarchical inference jointly over (population hyperparameters including mass-gap edges, EoS parameters, and cosmology including Hubble parameter H0), with selection effects for both GW detection and EM follow-up; propagate calibration and peculiar-velocity uncertainties in redshift.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
- Injection campaign: simulate BNS/NSBH/BBH events spanning the nominal 3–5 M⊙ mass gap, with realistic noise and varying EM follow-up completeness; compare recovered mass-gap occupancy, EoS posteriors, and H0 bias/variance against a baseline unconstrained PE pipeline (free Λ parameters, no TOV coupling, no EM likelihood).
- Posterior predictive checks: verify recovered Λ(m) curves satisfy nuclear-physics expectations; check consistency with independent constraints (NICER radii, heavy-ion bounds where applicable) without double-counting.
- Sensitivity analysis: quantify robustness to waveform systematics (different inspiral-tide models), to EM model uncertainty (ejecta-fit nuisance parameters), and to alert-threshold strategy via P_astro-weighted inclusion.
- Deliverables: constraints on mass-gap boundaries and occupancy, EoS posterior with credible bands for M–R–Λ, and an H0 posterior from standard sirens with explicitly reported systematic and selection-function budgets.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Inspiral waveforms encode tidal effects (Λ) that are deterministically linked to the neutron-star EoS via the TOV equations; enforcing causality/stability and the observed high-mass NS constraint substantially restricts Λ(m). Empirically, Virgo/LIGO observations plus GW170817-like multi-messenger events demonstrate that EM counterparts provide orthogonal information about ejecta that depends on compact-object type and masses, directly relevant to resolving ambiguous chirp-mass regions.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation embeds first-principles relativistic stellar-structure physics (TOV, causality) directly into parameter estimation instead of treating Λ as an unconstrained nuisance parameter. The trans-dimensional mixture structure matches the real astrophysical ambiguity between BNS/NSBH/BBH, especially in the mass gap, and the P_astro-weighted inclusion of low-significance candidates operationalizes the known purity-vs-FAR trade discussed in follow-up strategies.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to standard event-by-event PE, the constrained EoS manifold reduces degeneracies and prevents unphysical Λ solutions that mimic mass-gap objects; compared to GW-only hierarchical population models, the EM-coupled likelihood suppresses otherwise viable but EM-inconsistent NSBH/BNS interpretations, improving classification. Both effects improve distance–inclination inference and thereby reduce bias/uncertainty in the Hubble parameter from standard sirens while simultaneously tightening mass-gap population constraints.
Critique: This is a technically sophisticated and largely coherent proposal that embeds first-principles relativistic stellar-structure constraints directly into hierarchical GW+EM inference. The engineering plan is detailed and largely executable, particularly the EoS–TOV latent-function embedding and the trans-dimensional mixture model for compact-object type. The logical mechanism for degeneracy breaking (collapse of the Λ(m) manifold and EM-informed suppression of inconsistent mass-gap solutions) is sound and well motivated. Minor score deductions arise from (i) computational feasibility risks not being fully quantified—especially sampler efficiency and convergence under hard physical constraints and discrete latent variables—and (ii) some optimism in the impact of EM non-detections, given large uncertainties in ejecta modeling and viewing-angle dependence. These are not conceptual flaws but areas where the proposal slightly overstates robustness.

Hypothesis: A two-stage, energy-conserving kilonova inference framework that (i) treats the r-process “naked heating rate” q_naked(t) as a Ye–(s,τexp)-conditioned latent process with nuclear-data hyperparameters shared across events, and (ii) propagates that power through an explicitly parameterized, atomic-physics-anchored opacity model κ(Ye,T,ρ,λ) and a calibrated transport/discrepancy model, will yield falsifiable and unbiased constraints on lanthanide-poor ejecta (Mej, vej, Ye and X_Ln) despite geometry/viewing-angle uncertainty and radiative-transfer model mismatch. Mechanistically, identifiability comes from combining orthogonal observables that couple differently to the nuclear vs transport sectors: (a) late-time bolometric decline and band-to-band fading ratios constrain q_naked(t) and particle-dependent thermalization efficiencies f_i(t) once diffusion becomes sub-dominant; (b) contemporaneous color temperature and near-IR spectral line-blanketing/broad-feature indices constrain κ(λ) normalization and slope tied to lanthanide fraction and ionization state; and (c) photospheric radius evolution (from SED fits) constrains the diffusion time/geometry. The key advance over single-stage ‘effective heating’ fits is that κ(Ye,T,ρ,λ) is not allowed to flex arbitrarily: it is restricted to a minimal, physically interpretable basis with priors informed by atomic-structure calculations, while any residual mismatch between the semi-analytic diffusion module and Monte Carlo radiative transfer is captured by a separately calibrated discrepancy emulator. Degeneracy-breaking is therefore not asserted but pre-registered as a set of recovery benchmarks under controlled κ-flexibility, geometry/viewing-angle variation, and afterglow contamination. Finally, EOS-conditioning is included only insofar as it demonstrably increases expected information gain on (Mej, vej, geometry) and thus on thermalization/diffusion, quantified via Bayes factors and mutual-information increments relative to an EOS-agnostic baseline.
Plan:
Step 0 — Define observables and identifiability targets (pre-registered).
0.1 Observables vector per event: multi-band photometry (optical→NIR), optional spectra, and SED-derived summary statistics with propagated errors: (i) pseudo-bolometric luminosity L_bol(t) (with bandpass-dependent missing-flux uncertainty); (ii) color indices (e.g., g−r, r−i, i−J, J−H, H−K) as functions of time; (iii) SED-inferred color temperature T_c(t) and photospheric radius R_ph(t) with covariance; (iv) spectral “lanthanide blanketing indices” B_Ln(t) defined as flux ratios across broad NIR troughs (e.g., F(1.05–1.15µm)/F(1.25–1.35µm), F(1.45–1.55µm)/F(1.60–1.70µm)) and a continuum slope index S_NIR.
0.2 Pre-registered identifiability benchmarks (reported as coverage and bias): recovery of injected (median posterior error / true) for Ye, X_Ln, Mej, vej in synthetic tests under: (A) κ-model “minimal” flexibility; (B) κ-model “expanded” flexibility; (C) variable geometry and viewing angle; (D) with/without afterglow contamination; (E) with RT discrepancy turned on/off. Passing criterion: posterior 68% credible intervals achieve ≥60% empirical coverage and <0.3σ mean bias for Ye and log10 X_Ln; and Bayes factor prefers two-stage model over single-stage by lnK>5 in controlled injections where q_naked differs (Asset-2 regime).

Step 1 — Data assembly and uncertainty model.
1.1 Curate multi-event dataset: AT2017gfo plus JWST-quality GRB-associated KNe (e.g., GRB 230307A/AT 2023vfi-like) with consistent photometric calibration. Store: fluxes, calibration covariance (zero-point + bandpass), cadence gaps, host extinction priors, distance posteriors, and afterglow-monitoring constraints.
1.2 Likelihood includes: correlated photometric calibration nuisance parameters per instrument, extinction with R_V prior, distance marginalization, and an additive afterglow component per band modeled as F_AG(ν,t)=A_AG(ν/ν0)^{-β} (t/t0)^{-α} with priors from contemporaneous X-ray/optical afterglow fits (when available) or weakly informative priors otherwise.

Step 2 — Minimal explicit κ(Ye,T,ρ,λ) parameterization (atomic-physics-anchored).
2.1 Adopt a two-component ejecta model (blue/lanthanide-poor; red/lanthanide-rich). For each component c∈{b,r}, opacity is expressed as a low-dimensional basis capturing (i) overall normalization, (ii) wavelength slope/line-blanketing strength, and (iii) ionization/temperature transition:
κ_c(λ,T,ρ) = κ0,c · [ (λ/λ0)^{p_c} ] · [1 + a_c · S( (T−T_ion,c)/ΔT_c ) ] · (ρ/ρ0)^{u_c}.
Here S(x)=1/(1+e^{−x}) is a smooth transition encoding recombination/ionization-driven opacity change; κ0,c is baseline grey level; p_c captures NIR vs optical tilt (proxy for line density); a_c sets amplitude of the opacity jump across ionization; u_c is a weak density exponent (kept tightly prior-constrained).
2.2 Tie opacity parameters to composition with explicit, minimal composition mapping:
log10 κ0,c = A0,c + A_Ln · log10(X_Ln,c/X_ref)  with A_Ln>0,
T_ion,c = T0 + T_Ln · log10(X_Ln,c/X_ref),
p_c = p0 + p_Ln · log10(X_Ln,c/X_ref).
Blue component has prior X_Ln,b centered at 10^{−6}–10^{−4}; red at 10^{−3}–10^{−1} (broad but separated).
2.3 Atomic-physics-informed priors: (A_Ln, p_Ln, T_Ln, κ0 ranges) are assigned priors from lanthanide/actinide line-expansion opacity calculations (e.g., existing Kurucz/Tanaka/Kasen-style tables). Practically: fit the above basis to a published grid of κ(λ,T,ρ) tables across representative compositions to derive prior means/covariances; use those as Gaussian priors with inflation factor (e.g., ×2) to remain conservative.
2.4 Forecast separability (mandatory): before fitting data, run Fisher / mutual-information forecasts on a representative cadence + filter set (optical + NIR + JWST bands) to quantify which epochs/bands constrain (κ0,p,T_ion) independently of q_naked hyperparameters. Deliverable: heatmaps of expected MI(κ-params; data|model) and MI(q_naked-params; data|model) vs time and wavelength; identify a minimal “anchor” set of bands/epochs needed (e.g., ≥1 optical band at t<0.7 d plus ≥2 NIR bands at t≈1–7 d, plus at least one spectrum or two NIR color indices around recombination).

Step 3 — Stage A: nuclear heating latent process q_naked(t).
3.1 Precompute r-process network library across (Ye,s,τexp) for both dynamical ejecta and disk winds; store channel-decomposed specific heating:
q_naked(t)= Σ_i q_i(t),  i∈{β,e−,ν̄ losses; α; fission; γ}.
Also store emitted particle energy distributions needed for thermalization.
3.2 Emulator: train a conditional normalizing flow or GP with monotonic/time-smoothness regularization to output {q_i(t)} on a log-time grid. Inputs: (Ye, s, τexp) plus nuclear hyperparameters θ_nuc (mass model index, β-strength scaling, fission yield family). Output uncertainty includes emulator error + nuclear-model ensemble variance.
3.3 Shared hyperparameters: θ_nuc are population-level parameters inferred jointly across events; event-level latents include Ye,c distributions (e.g., Beta distribution parameters per component) and mixing fraction between components.

Step 4 — Stage B: deposition + transport with explicit discrepancy calibrated to Monte Carlo RT.
4.1 Thermalization (energy deposition): for each particle channel i, use a physics-motivated efficiency function
f_i(t|Mej,vej,B_trap,χ_e)= [1 + (t/t0,i)^{n_i}]^{−1},
with t0,i ∝ (Mej/vej^2)^{1/2} scaled by composition-dependent electron density proxy χ_e (linked to Ye) and magnetic trapping parameter B_trap (log-uniform prior over a conservative range). Enforce 0≤f_i≤1 and correct asymptotics; allow small multiplicative nuisance per channel (≤20%) to account for microphysics uncertainty.
q_dep(t)= Σ_i f_i(t) q_i(t).
4.2 Baseline diffusion/SED model (explicit): use a two-component Arnett-style homologous-expansion diffusion model with time-dependent photosphere, but multi-band emission approximated by a diluted blackbody with wavelength-dependent attenuation via κ(λ,T,ρ):
L_c(t) computed from diffusion equation with t_d,c ∝ (κ̄_c Mej,c / vej,c c)^{1/2} and geometric factor g(Ω_c,θ_view).
Spectral flux: F_λ(t) = Σ_c [ (R_ph,c(t)^2 / D^2) · ζ_c(t) · B_λ(T_c(t)) · exp(−τ_eff,c(λ,t)) ],
where τ_eff uses κ_c(λ,T,ρ) and homologous density profile. ζ_c is a color-correction factor with tight priors from RT comparisons.
4.3 Transport/discrepancy emulator (mandatory): calibrate residuals against a grid of Monte Carlo RT simulations spanning (Mej,vej,X_Ln,geometry,θ_view) and representative heating inputs.
Define residual process in log-flux space per band:
Δ_m(t,band) = log F_RT − log F_diff,
modeled as a GP or low-rank basis with coefficients predicted by a trained emulator E_Δ(params). In inference, predicted flux is F_pred=F_diff·exp(Δ_m), with Δ_m marginalized using the calibrated uncertainty. This prevents attributing RT mismatch to q_naked or κ.
4.4 Geometry/viewing-angle: include a minimal anisotropy parameterization (two-zone solid angles Ω_b,Ω_r and viewing angle θ_view) with priors informed by NR/RT studies; geometry enters both diffusion time (via g) and effective column density in τ_eff. Crucially, discrepancy emulator is trained across the same geometry range.

Step 5 — EOS-conditioned priors and incremental value quantification.
5.1 EOS-conditioned prior construction: map EOS parameters (subject to causality + M_max constraints) to plausible ejecta priors using NR-calibrated surrogate relations (e.g., Mej_dyn(R1.4,q), vej_dyn(R1.4,q), disk mass) and to Ye support for disk winds. Include GW-inferred constraints when available; otherwise use broad EOS prior.
5.2 Mandatory incremental-value test: run paired analyses for each event and for the population: (i) EOS-agnostic priors; (ii) EOS-conditioned priors (with/without GW constraints). Report expected information gain ΔI on (Mej,vej,θ_view) and downstream ΔI on Ye and X_Ln; compute Bayes factors for models with EOS-conditioning vs without, ensuring complexity is justified.

Step 6 — Inference engine and diagnostics.
6.1 Perform joint Bayesian inference with hierarchical structure: event-level parameters {Mej,c, vej,c, Ye,c distribution, X_Ln,c, Ω_c, θ_view, afterglow nuisances}; population-level θ_nuc and κ-basis hyperparameters (with atomic priors). Sampling via NUTS with reparameterizations (non-centered for hierarchical parts) or SMC with amortized proposals.
6.2 Degeneracy quantification: compute posterior mutual information and correlation structure among {q_naked hyperparameters, κ parameters, Mej, Ye, X_Ln} and compare against a baseline single-stage effective-heating model. Pre-register that success means a statistically significant reduction in posterior dependence corr(q_naked,κ) and improved coverage in synthetic recovery.

Step 7 — Validation program (falsifiable, mismatch-resistant).
7.1 Synthetic injections: generate mock datasets from Monte Carlo RT (not from the diffusion model) across controlled scenarios matching the pre-registered benchmarks in Step 0. Recover parameters under (a) correct κ-basis; (b) expanded κ-basis; (c) misspecified κ-basis; and with/without discrepancy emulator. Report failure modes explicitly.
7.2 Real-event cross-validation: fit early-time-only data (e.g., t<1 d) and predict late-time (t>1 d and JWST epochs), focusing on the Asset-2 regime (Ye≳0.3, late times). Score predictive log-likelihood and calibration of credible intervals.
7.3 Nuclear stress tests: rerun with alternative nuclear mass models/fission yields; quantify which θ_nuc drive q_naked differences in the inferred Ye range; propagate to Ye and X_Ln posteriors.
7.4 Deliverables: (i) public emulator for q_naked and RT discrepancy; (ii) κ-basis fits and priors derived from atomic tables; (iii) posterior samples for each event; (iv) a “bias map” showing how common heating-rate mis-specifications bias Mej,vej,Ye when κ is constrained vs unconstrained.

Milestones (practical):
M1: κ-basis + atomic prior fit + MI/Fisher forecast deliverable.
M2: RT grid + discrepancy emulator with documented error envelopes.
M3: End-to-end hierarchical inference on synthetic RT injections meeting coverage criteria.
M4: Multi-event real-data analysis with EOS-value quantification (Bayes factors / ΔI).
Feasibility:
Addressing the reviewer’s core concern—degeneracy-breaking being under-specified—the revised plan makes identifiability falsifiable and robust to mismatch in four concrete ways.

(1) Minimal explicit κ(Ye,T,ρ,λ) with atomic priors (degeneracy is not shifted into an unconstrained κ): κ is restricted to a low-dimensional, interpretable basis (normalization κ0, wavelength tilt p, and an ionization-transition term via T_ion and amplitude a) with composition-linked mappings to X_Ln. Priors are not hand-wavy; they are obtained by fitting this basis to published atomic-structure opacity tables and carried into inference as Gaussian priors (inflated conservatively). This directly answers the critique that a too-flexible κ would reintroduce the heating/opacity degeneracy.

(2) Orthogonal leverage is demonstrated before fitting (not asserted): Fisher/mutual-information forecasts on the actual cadence+filters quantify which epochs/bands/spectral indices constrain κ separately from q_naked. This operationalizes the claim that late-time slopes and NIR blanketing indices disentangle nuclear vs opacity/ionization effects, and it yields a concrete observing/inference requirement (minimum band/epoch set) rather than a qualitative argument.

(3) Transport approximation is specified and protected by a calibrated discrepancy model: the diffusion/SED module is explicitly defined (two-component Arnett-like diffusion plus wavelength-dependent attenuation). Crucially, any systematic mismatch relative to Monte Carlo RT is not absorbed by q_naked or κ because a residual emulator Δ_m(params,t,band) is trained on an RT grid and marginalized during inference. This prevents HMC/SMC from becoming overconfident and misattributing RT errors to nuclear-heating features—directly satisfying the mandatory directive.

(4) EOS-conditioning is justified quantitatively, not by appeal: the proposal commits to paired analyses (EOS-agnostic vs EOS-conditioned, with/without GW constraints) and reports Bayes factors and expected information gain on (Mej,vej,geometry) and downstream (Ye,X_Ln). If EOS-conditioning does not increase information in a measurable way, it will be removed or down-weighted; thus it cannot become a complexity add-on that drives results by prior.

Empirical and literature grounding (Assets 1–2): Asset 2 motivates explicit treatment of q_naked in the Ye≳0.3, t≳1 d regime where standard heating prescriptions bias inference; Asset 1 demonstrates that composition differences (lanthanide-poor vs rich) have observable consequences and that JWST-quality data are sufficiently constraining to meaningfully test these models, including heavy-element synthesis pathways. The revised framework translates these motivations into a constrained statistical architecture with pre-registered recovery benchmarks and an RT-calibrated discrepancy channel, making the central claim testable and resilient to model mismatch.
Critique: This is an unusually thorough and technically mature proposal. The engineering plan is exceptionally detailed, specifying concrete parameterizations, priors, emulators, discrepancy modeling, and validation benchmarks. Logical consistency is strong: the separation of nuclear heating from transport is well-motivated, identifiability is not assumed but pre-registered and stress-tested, and degeneracy control is addressed via both physical priors and discrepancy emulation. Minor deductions arise from the cumulative complexity: the simultaneous inference of nuclear hyperparameters, opacity bases, geometry, EOS-conditioning, and discrepancy processes risks practical identifiability and sampler pathologies even with careful reparameterization. While acknowledged and partially mitigated, the proposal would benefit from a clearer minimal viable configuration demonstrating success before full hierarchical generalization. Evidence grounding is solid and remains within nuclear astrophysics and radiative transfer; atomic-physics priors and r-process network references are appropriate and not speculative. The rationale is strong, representing a genuine structural advance over effective-heating fits rather than an incremental application.

Hypothesis: Type II–like burst trains with QPOs can be explained by a small, explicitly enumerated class of relaxation oscillators in the inner accretion flow, but the driver is not assumed a priori to be an oscillating radiation-pressure shock. Instead, we hypothesize that (H1) shock-gated inner-flow oscillations, (H2) magnetospheric gating/propeller cycles, and (H3) disk thermal–viscous limit cycles occupy distinct, falsifiable regions in a joint observable space spanned by (i) νQPO–hardness and νQPO–energy-dependent rms relations, (ii) burst rise/decay scalings with dynamical vs viscous timescales, (iii) harmonic content and phase lags of the QPO through the burst phase, and (iv) recurrence–fluence–persistent-luminosity scaling. The central claim is that mechanistic identifiability becomes achievable when the inference model hard-codes each mechanism’s governing timescale, energy reservoir, and closure (including radiative source terms), and when the νQPO mapping is fixed to pre-registered, mechanistically derived relations rather than being left flexible. For the shock-gated hypothesis specifically, we adopt a GR-aware, radiatively cooled, vertically integrated inner-flow model with an effective (but validated) radiative-hydrodynamic jump condition; the burst sharp decay is predicted to track a post-shock advective drainage time tdec ~ tad(Rs), and νQPO is predicted to track the inverse of the same advective/infall time with a fixed scaling that implies a tight νQPO–tdec anticorrelation and a specific phase relation between flux and hardness. For neutron stars, we further hypothesize that a thermonuclear module is required (and statistically preferred) precisely in regimes where the peak-to-persistent luminosity ratio β controls cooling-tail detectability (as in IGR J17480-2446): the model will attribute non-cooling thermonuclear bursts to high persistent backgrounds and lower peak temperatures without misclassifying them as accretion-gated events. Peak luminosity is treated with mechanism-specific caps: a photospheric/local Eddington-limited cap with redshift and composition dependence for NS, versus a geometry/Comptonization-limited phenomenological cap for BH candidates. Finally, EOS inference is posed not as ‘tighter by default’ but as a hierarchical constraint that is only claimed when posterior predictive checks demonstrate that nuisance parameters (distance, anisotropy, color correction, composition) do not dominate the compactness posterior; otherwise the outcome is a principled null result that still yields robust burst-mechanism classification.
Plan:
Step 0 — Pre-registration (discriminating predictions and model roster)
0.1 Enumerate competing mechanisms as explicit state-space models: H1 shock-gated inner flow; H2 magnetospheric gating/propeller; H3 disk thermal–viscous limit cycle; plus H4 thermonuclear-only (NS control) and H5 hybrid (accretion gating + nuclear burning). Freeze the model list and decision criteria before fitting.
0.2 Pre-register discriminants computed from data and posterior predictive simulations:
  - D1: νQPO–tdec scaling: shock model predicts νQPO ∝ 1/tad(Rs) and tdec ≈ κ tad(Rs) ⇒ νQPO tdec ≈ const (with scatter from inclination/spectral decomposition); magnetospheric gating predicts νQPO tied to νK(Rm) while decay reflects emptying of inner disk/boundary layer with weaker νQPO–tdec coupling.
  - D2: Energy-dependent QPO rms and phase lags: shock/hot-flow predicts stronger rms at higher energies with hard lags set by Comptonization time; disk limit-cycle predicts softer rms dominance and different lag sign/energy trend.
  - D3: Harmonic content: shock oscillations predict specific harmonic ratios dependent on compression ratio C (e.g., stronger 2nd harmonic when oscillation is non-sinusoidal); gating predicts harmonics linked to switching/nonlinearity at Rm.
  - D4: Recurrence–fluence relation: shock/gating predicts burst fluence scales with refilled reservoir in inner flow ~ ∫(ṁin−ṁout)dt, with tight correlation to recurrence; nuclear predicts fluence ~ y Qnuc with ignition physics and distinct dependence on persistent luminosity.

Step 1 — Dataset construction, uniform reduction, and derived observables
1.1 Sources:
  - BH candidate: GRS 1915+105 quasi-regular bursts with sharp decay and contemporaneous QPOs (per Asset 2).
  - NS set: (a) type II candidates (e.g., Rapid Burster/MXB 1730−335 and/or Bursting Pulsar GRO J1744−28 if included in the archive), (b) thermonuclear controls across accretion regimes, and (c) IGR J17480-2446-like high persistent luminosity regimes where β governs cooling detectability (per Asset 1).
1.2 Data products (mission-dependent; RXTE/ASTROSAT/NICER where available):
  - Light curves in ≥3 energy bands (soft/medium/hard) with deadtime correction, background modeling, and barycentering.
  - Time-resolved spectra with forward-folding response; extract spectral parameters with two decompositions: (S1) disk+Comptonization, (S2) blackbody+Comptonization (NS), carrying decomposition uncertainty forward as a discrete latent choice or mixture.
  - Sliding-window power spectra (e.g., 1–16 s windows stepped by 0.25–1 s), tracking νQPO, Q, and fractional rms vs energy band.
  - Burst-shape features with uncertainties: rise time, tdec (e.g., e-folding or sharp-drop timescale), fluence, peak flux, β = Lpeak/Lpers, hardness evolution, and QPO phase-resolved amplitude.

Step 2 — Mechanism-specific state-space models (architectural specificity)
All models share: observation model for multi-band count rates and spectral/hardness proxies; latent states evolve via SDE/ODE; a joint likelihood fits light curve + hardness/spectral temperature + νQPO(t) + energy-dependent rms.

2.1 H1 Shock-gated inner-flow oscillator (radiatively cooled, GR-aware effective closure)
2.1.1 Latent states: Rs(t) (shock radius), C(t) (compression), Σin(t) (inner-disk surface density), ṁin(t), and Te(t)/τ(t) (Comptonizing electron temperature/optical depth proxy) to link to hardness/rms.
2.1.2 Fixed νQPO mapping (pre-registered): adopt the post-shock advective/infall timescale in a pseudo-Newtonian potential as baseline, with a single scaling parameter ξ (order unity) shared across bursts within a source:
  - tad(Rs) = ∫_{Rin}^{Rs} dr / |vr(r)| with vr from the vertically integrated momentum equation in the chosen potential.
  - νQPO(t) = [2π ξ tad(Rs(t))]^{-1}.
Falsifiable predictions: (P1) νQPO increases as Rs decreases during refill/drain cycle; (P2) tdec tracks tad at collapse; (P3) νQPO–hardness correlation sign set by Te/τ response to ṁin and Rs.
2.1.3 Shock “jump” closure and source terms:
  - Use an effective radiative-hydrodynamic jump condition for vertically integrated flow:
    * Mass: [ρ v] = 0.
    * Momentum: [Pgas + Prad + ρ v^2] = 0, with optional Pmag term toggled off/on (Bayesian model variant H1a no-B, H1b with-B).
    * Energy: include an explicit radiative loss term across the shock: [ (1/2)v^2 + h ] = −Δqrad, where Δqrad is parameterized by a cooling function Λ = Λ0 ρ^2 T^α (effective Compton/bremsstrahlung) with α and Λ0 given informative priors from hot-flow literature; this replaces vague “penalty conservation”.
  - Radiation pressure included via Prad = (a/3) T^4 with a color-correction/Comptonization bridge to observed hardness; vertical leakage approximated by a flux-limited cooling term in the energy equation rather than enforcing adiabatic RH.
2.1.4 Differentiability strategy for shock transitions:
  - Replace discontinuous switching with a continuous relaxation: enforce jump constraints via a smooth barrier/soft-constraint with temperature parameter ε (annealed during inference), and represent “collapse” events as rapid but continuous trajectories in Rs governed by stiff ODE (solved implicitly).
2.1.5 Emission mapping:
  - Persistent emission from ṁ and coronal parameters; burst component proportional to transient increase in ṁin through inner region (not Eddington-capped for BH by default; see Step 2.4).

2.2 H2 Magnetospheric gating/propeller cycle (NS-specific; strong alternative)
2.2.1 Latent states: Rm(t) (magnetospheric radius), ṁ(t) at inner disk, ΔMin(t) (stored mass in inner disk reservoir), Ω* (spin; prior from pulsations if known), μ (magnetic dipole moment).
2.2.2 Dynamics:
  - Rm ∝ μ^{4/7} (GM)^{−1/7} ṁ^{−2/7} with stochastic ṁ(t) driven by outer supply.
  - Gating condition via fastness ωs = Ω*/ΩK(Rm). When ωs crosses ~1, accretion switches to partial/blocked with a smooth sigmoid (continuous relaxation to preserve differentiability).
2.2.3 Observable predictions:
  - νQPO tied to νK(Rm) or beat-frequency forms (enumerated and fixed as two sub-variants H2a/H2b); predicts different νQPO–hardness and νQPO–tdec relations than H1.
  - Burst fluence set by reservoir emptying ΔMin; recurrence controlled by refilling time ~ ΔMin/ṁsupply.

2.3 H3 Disk thermal–viscous limit cycle (radiation-pressure instability)
2.3.1 Latent states: Σ(t), Tin(t), Rin(t) or an effective inner disk temperature and surface density; αvisc as parameter with informative prior.
2.3.2 Dynamics:
  - Use a reduced S-curve normal form (bistable ODE) calibrated to reproduce limit-cycle timescales; recurrence scales with viscous time tvisc ~ R^2/ν.
2.3.3 Observables:
  - Spectral softening/hardening sequence and QPO behavior predicted to correlate with disk state; QPO not forced to track an advective timescale as in H1.

2.4 Luminosity cap modeling (mechanism- and object-specific)
2.4.1 NS: photospheric/local Eddington cap with composition X and GR redshift:
  - FEdd,loc = (c g / κ) with κ≈0.2(1+X) cm^2/g; observed flux includes redshift and anisotropy: Fobs = (FEdd,loc / (1+z)^2) × ξb^{-1} × fcol^{-4} (implemented via standard color correction mapping in spectral model).
2.4.2 BH: no universal Eddington ceiling enforced. Instead, introduce a geometry/Comptonization cap parameter Lcap,BH with prior wide and correlated with hardness/τ to allow saturation via optical depth, beaming, or spectral pivoting—explicitly preventing NS-style Eddington assumptions from biasing BH fits.

2.5 Thermonuclear module and Asset-1 linkage (NS)
2.5.1 Latent states: fuel column y(t), base heating Qb, composition (X, Z) with priors; ignition/depletion as in reduced ignition models.
2.5.2 Cooling-tail detectability modeled explicitly: predicted observed temperature decay competes with persistent background; the model predicts when cooling is undetectable as a function of β and background, reproducing the Asset-1 result that cooling is sufficient but not necessary for thermonuclear classification.
2.5.3 Hybrid H5 allows simultaneous gating and nuclear burning; Bayes factors decide necessity.

Step 3 — Inference strategy for stiff constrained dynamics
3.1 Primary inference engine: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) / particle MCMC for state trajectories with stiff dynamics; HMC/NUTS reserved for lower-dimensional static parameters conditional on trajectories (or via marginal likelihood approximations). Rationale: discontinuity-like behavior and multimodality make pure HMC fragile.
3.2 Numerics:
  - Implicit integrator (e.g., BDF) for stiff ODE components with adjoint sensitivities for gradients where used.
  - Anneal constraint temperature ε and gating sigmoid sharpness to transition from smooth to near-physical regimes while maintaining sampler stability.
3.3 Model comparison:
  - Use PSIS-LOO and held-out burst-trains predictive likelihood for within-source validation; compute Bayes factors only where marginal likelihood estimates are stable (bridge sampling/SMC evidence).

Step 4 — Systematics and hierarchical treatment (EOS realism)
4.1 Nuisance parameters (hierarchical priors): distance D, inclination i, anisotropy factors (ξp, ξb), color correction fcol, and spectral decomposition choice (mixture between S1/S2). Priors from literature where available; otherwise weakly informative with physically bounded supports.
4.2 Propagate systematics into FEdd and compactness:
  - Fit NS sources jointly with partial pooling on (fcol, ξb) and composition hyperpriors; allow source-to-source variation.
4.3 Simulation-based calibration (SBC): generate synthetic datasets with known (M,R) and nuisance parameters; demonstrate regimes where (M,R) is recoverable versus nuisance-dominated; predefine a success criterion (e.g., median posterior width in compactness GM/Rc^2 improves by ≥X% over prior while maintaining calibration).

Step 5 — Falsification / posterior predictive criteria (non-negotiable)
5.1 If a mechanism wins by evidence, it must also pass: (a) reproducing νQPO phase evolution and energy-dependent rms, (b) reproducing observed νQPO–tdec and νQPO–hardness scaling, and (c) reproducing recurrence–fluence scaling.
5.2 If shock model H1 is selected, require that inferred Rs(t) and C(t) imply physically plausible Mach numbers and optical depths under the adopted closure; otherwise reject H1 even if fit quality is high (guard against ‘fit-driven’ Rs).
5.3 For NS thermonuclear cases: require that nuclear energy release and α = (persistent fluence between bursts)/(burst fluence) fall in thermonuclear ranges; for accretion-gated cases require consistency with gravitational energy budget.

- A reusable probabilistic program implementing H1–H5 with SMC/particle MCMC backend.
- Source-by-source mechanism classification with uncertainty, plus (conditional) NS compactness constraints where systematics permit.
Feasibility:
Addresses (i) incomplete comparison space: The revised plan explicitly implements magnetospheric gating/propeller and disk thermal–viscous limit-cycle models as first-class alternatives with their own latent states, dynamics, and predicted observables, preventing confirmation by omission. Discriminants (phase lags, harmonic structure, energy-dependent QPO rms, recurrence–fluence scaling) are pre-registered and evaluated via posterior predictive checks, not post-hoc interpretation.

Addresses (ii) νQPO mapping ambiguity: The proposal now fixes a single primary Rs→νQPO relation (advective/infall timescale) for H1, with at most a small enumerated set of alternatives only in the magnetospheric model (νK vs beat-frequency). This creates falsifiable predictions, especially the νQPO–tdec anticorrelation and the sign/strength of νQPO–hardness coupling, reducing the risk that flexible mappings absorb discrepancies.

Addresses (iii) shock-physics closure: Rather than enforcing generic ‘conservation penalties’, the shock model specifies an effective equation of state including radiation pressure and an explicit radiative loss term Δqrad with a parameterized cooling law. Magnetic pressure is treated as an explicit toggle (H1a/H1b), making assumptions transparent and testable. The closure is positioned as ‘effective’ and will be validated via synthetic data from GR(R)HD-inspired toy simulations and simulation-based calibration, ensuring the constraints match the intended physics.

Addresses (iv) luminosity caps BH vs NS: The model enforces an Eddington/redshift/composition cap only for NS photospheric-limited emission. BH candidates instead use a geometry/Comptonization-limited saturation parameterization, avoiding biased inference from an inappropriate Eddington ceiling.

Addresses (v) EOS optimism and systematics: EOS inference is conditional and hierarchical, with explicit nuisance parameters (distance, anisotropy, color correction, composition, spectral decomposition) marginalized rather than fixed. Simulation-based calibration is used to demonstrate whether compactness constraints are identifiable in realistic regimes; otherwise the project still produces a robust classification of burst mechanism and quantitative constraints on timescales/energy budgets.

Computational tractability: Recognizing stiffness and near-discontinuous behavior, the inference plan prioritizes SMC/particle MCMC for latent trajectories, uses implicit integrators, and employs continuous relaxations (annealed barriers/sigmoids) to preserve differentiability and stabilize posterior geometry. Clear falsification criteria are defined so that good fits that violate mechanistic predictions are rejected.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and technically mature proposal. Its primary strength lies in methodological explicitness: competing mechanisms are enumerated, νQPO mappings are fixed a priori, and falsification criteria are non-negotiable. The shock-gated model is treated as an effective but testable physical closure rather than a phenomenological fit, which substantially mitigates historical ambiguities in type II burst interpretation. Minor score deductions arise from (i) the reliance on vertically integrated and pseudo-Newtonian treatments for intrinsically GRMHD-scale phenomena, which may limit physical fidelity in extreme regimes, and (ii) the significant computational and implementation complexity, which poses execution risk despite being conceptually well justified. These issues do not undermine logical validity but temper confidence in full empirical delivery within typical grant timelines.

Hypothesis: A first-order, strong-coupling phase transition in supranuclear matter (n ≳ 1.5–3 ns) generically produces a “spin-dependent maximum mass gap” that separates long-lived hypermassive neutron-star remnants from prompt-collapse black holes in compact binary mergers; this gap imprints itself as a correlated boundary in the joint distribution of (i) remnant collapse time (and thus EM/neutrino activity), (ii) the lightest black hole mass in the post-merger population, and (iii) the observed effective inspiral spin parameter χ_eff for events near the NS–BH/BBH boundary. Mechanism: in strong-coupling EoS with a latent-heat-driven softening followed by quark-matter stiffening, the threshold mass for collapse depends sharply on angular momentum support; because χ_eff partially encodes pre-merger aligned spin angular momentum, it modulates the available centrifugal support and shifts the collapse threshold, creating a detectable χ_eff-dependent cutoff in the lightest black hole mass. Methodological adaptation: replace standard population+waveform inference (which treats EoS and spin effects as weakly coupled nuisance structure) with a physics-constrained, differentiable hierarchical inference pipeline that (a) embeds a hybrid strong-coupling EoS family (e.g., V-QCD-calibrated) into a differentiable TOV + rapid-rotation + collapse-threshold surrogate, and (b) couples this surrogate directly to gravitational-wave likelihoods via a χ_eff-conditioned collapse-threshold prior that is strictly constrained by causality, thermodynamic stability, and GR equilibrium/turning-point conditions.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Compile GW posterior samples for BBH/NSBH/BNS candidates from public catalogs (e.g., GWTC releases), retaining joint posteriors over component masses, spins, χ_eff, and (where available) tidal parameters and merger/ringdown quantities.
1.2 Curate a “boundary sample” focused on systems with secondary masses in the 2–5 M⊙ range and/or ambiguous classification; include GW190814-like events explicitly.
1.3 Assemble external constraints: (i) 2 M⊙ pulsar masses, (ii) NICER mass–radius posteriors, (iii) nuclear-theory low-density priors up to ~ns, and (iv) optional kilonova/GRB afterglow constraints that inform prompt collapse vs remnant survival.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Strong-coupling EoS embedding: build an EoS parameterization that interpolates from chiral-EFT-consistent nuclear matter at n≲ns to a V-QCD-motivated high-density sector with an explicit first-order transition (parameters: transition density, latent heat/Δε, quark-phase stiffness/sound speed profile). Enforce hard constraints: dp/dε > 0 (stability), cs^2 ≤ 1 (causality), thermodynamic consistency, and correct matching conditions across the transition.
2.2 Differentiable GR structure and rotation surrogate (methodological adaptation):
- Implement a differentiable TOV solver for non-rotating sequences producing M(R), M_TOV, and baryonic mass mapping.
- Construct a rapid-rotation and merger-remnant support model that outputs M_max(J) and the threshold mass for prompt collapse M_th(J, EoS). Instead of using a fixed universal relation (e.g., Breu–Rezzolla) as a post-hoc check, learn an EoS-conditional surrogate with built-in monotonicity and turning-point stability constraints (∂M/∂ρc = 0 at onset of instability) using a constrained architecture (e.g., monotone neural spline layers) trained on a limited grid of full GR rapid-rotation solutions (RNS/LORENE) for sampled EoS.
- Couple angular momentum at merger J to inspiral observables by mapping (m1,m2,χ_eff) → J via PN/EOB-informed relations with calibration factors; treat spin misalignment through an explicit nuisance distribution constrained by χ_eff posteriors rather than assuming aligned spins.
2.3 χ_eff-conditioned collapse-threshold prior: define a physically motivated latent variable z = “prompt collapse vs remnant” with probability P(z|m1,m2,χ_eff,EoS) determined by whether total mass exceeds M_th(J,EoS). This couples χ_eff to whether the outcome is a black hole immediately (lightest BH formation) or a massive NS remnant (with possible delayed collapse).
2.4 Hierarchical Bayesian inference (core adapted pipeline): perform joint inference over (i) EoS/phase-transition parameters, (ii) population hyperparameters for masses and spin distributions (allowing anti-aligned χ_eff fractions), and (iii) event-level classification z, using the full GW likelihood (or posterior reweighting with selection effects). Unlike standard hierarchical fits, the likelihood is reweighted by the differentiable, constraint-respecting remnant model so that EoS parameters directly modulate inferred rates near the maximum-mass boundary.
2.5 Selection and detectability modeling: incorporate detection efficiency as a function of masses and spins; explicitly test how χ_eff-dependent SNR biases could mimic a cutoff, and include these biases in the hierarchical model.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Internal consistency checks: verify recovered EoS obeys causality and stability at all densities; confirm M_TOV and M_max/M_TOV distributions reproduce known bounds in limiting cases (no transition, weak transition).
3.2 Injection campaigns: generate synthetic populations with/without a first-order strong-coupling transition and with varying anti-aligned spin fractions; run end-to-end recovery to quantify Bayes factors, false-positive rates for detecting χ_eff-dependent cutoffs, and identifiability of (transition density, latent heat, quark stiffness).
3.3 Cross-messenger validation: for events with EM counterparts or constraints on prompt collapse, compare inferred z with EM-informed remnant survival; check whether inferred EoS predicts consistent disk masses/ejecta qualitatively (via established fitting formulae).
3.4 Mechanism-specific tests: measure the inferred slope of the “lightest BH mass vs χ_eff boundary” and test the predicted sign: more positive χ_eff (more aligned spin support) should shift the collapse threshold upward, reducing the probability of forming the lightest BH at fixed masses; a strong first-order transition should sharpen this boundary relative to purely hadronic EoS.
3.5 Comparative baselines: compare against (i) standard broken power-law mass models without EoS coupling, and (ii) EoS inference that uses only tidal deformability without outcome-class coupling, quantifying improvements in constraints on M_TOV, M_max/M_TOV, and the existence/location of the phase transition.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Strong-coupling EoS models with first-order transitions (e.g., V-QCD-like) can raise M_max/M_TOV and alter remnant stability, while GW catalogs already show nontrivial χ_eff structure including anti-aligned spins; near the 2–5 M⊙ boundary, small changes in rotational support can qualitatively change the outcome (NS remnant vs BH).
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The key limitation in current analyses is the weak or post-hoc coupling between inspiral-measured spin (χ_eff), dense-matter microphysics (EoS/phase transitions), and the collapse outcome that sets the lightest black hole mass. Embedding a constraint-enforcing, differentiable GR+rotation surrogate into hierarchical inference allows direct propagation of strong-coupling EoS parameters into observable population features while guaranteeing causality and stability.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to unconstrained regression or purely phenomenological population models, the adapted pipeline (i) prevents unphysical EoS solutions via hard architectural constraints, (ii) leverages χ_eff as mechanistic information about angular-momentum support rather than a descriptive parameter, and (iii) converts ambiguous “lightest black hole vs heavy neutron star” cases into quantitative evidence for/against strong-coupling phase transitions through a χ_eff-conditioned collapse-threshold imprint, improving identifiability of the maximum mass and transition parameters under realistic selection effects.
Critique: This is a technically sophisticated and largely well-justified proposal that directly targets a real bottleneck in compact-object population inference: the disconnect between inspiral spin measurements, dense-matter microphysics, and post-merger outcomes. The strong-coupling first-order transition mechanism is physically plausible and the logical chain from latent-heat softening → angular-momentum-sensitive collapse threshold → χ_eff-dependent lightest-BH boundary is internally consistent. Engineering execution is unusually detailed, particularly the constrained differentiable surrogate for M_th(J,EoS), and reflects current best practices in GR+ML hybrid modeling. Score deductions arise primarily from (i) residual degeneracy risks between χ_eff-dependent selection effects and true collapse-threshold physics, which may be harder to break than implied even with hierarchical modeling, and (ii) the reliance on PN/EOB-informed mappings from χ_eff to merger angular momentum J, which are still approximate and could dilute the sharpness of the predicted boundary. While these are acknowledged, the proposal somewhat overstates identifiability given current catalog sizes.

Hypothesis: Neutron-star EOS stiffness determines the radial stratification ρ(r), pressure scale height H(r), and composition gradients that set the local Alfvén frequency spectrum ωA(r) and buoyancy coupling, which in turn control (a) the onset/saturation of Tayler-type non-axisymmetric instabilities and (b) the efficiency with which internal mixed poloidal–toroidal reconfiguration transmits (or fails to transmit) magnetic flux through the crust into the exterior. When the crust–magnetosphere matching is treated with an explicit, physics-based closure (elastic crust + resistive/Hall induction in the crust + resistive/force-free exterior), the resulting time-dependent external multipole content and effective dipole moment μeff(t) becomes a well-defined, gauge-invariant observable of the interior evolution rather than a tunable functional. We hypothesize that, at fixed accreted mass and spin, EOS-dependent stratification shifts the instability saturation into distinct regimes of μeff(t) amplitude and variability: (i) a “stable-channeling” regime with sufficiently persistent μeff(t) enabling coherent AMXP pulsations, (ii) a “variable-magnetosphere” regime with enhanced low-frequency μeff(t) fluctuations that elevate torque-noise/pulse-phase wander and modify disk truncation, and (iii) a “weak-external-field” endpoint after accretion/cooling that maps onto the RMSP dipole distribution. Because Hall drift and temperature-dependent resistivity introduce characteristic timescale/phase signatures that differ from pure EOS-driven changes (Hall: dispersive spectral transfer across ℓ; resistive: monotonic damping with known T scaling), jointly fitting μeff(t) statistics, truncation-radius variability, and radio/X-ray jet diagnostics can disentangle EOS stiffness from transport microphysics. The refined approach overcomes the reviewers’ identifiability concern by (1) replacing parameterized magnetosphere/jet closures with explicit crust-to-exterior matching that uniquely defines μeff(t), (2) including the leading non-ideal terms (Hall + η(T,Qi)) and crustal elasticity that control flux transmission during/after accretion, and (3) pre-registering sensitivity/degeneracy tests (Fisher/adjoint) that quantify which EOS density bands are constrained by which observables and under what sample size and systematic budgets.
Plan:
Step 0 — Scope control and parameterization (pre-registered):
