0.1 EOS parameterization (piecewise polytrope): Use a 3–4 segment piecewise-polytropic core joined to a fixed crust EOS. Inference parameters: {Γ1,Γ2,Γ3, ρ12,ρ23} (or equivalent pressure-at-fixed-density nodes), with hard priors enforcing thermodynamic stability and causality (0 < c_s^2 ≤ c^2) and Mmax ≥ 2 M⊙.
0.2 Transport/microphysics parameters (explicit, minimal but non-ideal):
  • Hall: include Hall term with electron number density ne(r) from the stratification; treat an uncertainty scale factor fHall multiplying ne (bounded prior) to represent composition/superconductivity uncertainty.
  • Resistivity: η(r,T)=η0(r;Qi) (T/T0)^α with α pre-set by dominant scattering regime; nuisance parameters: impurity parameter Qi (bounded) and normalization η0 scale factor fη.
  • Thermal evolution: a minimal, observable-informed T(t) model: outburst heating + exponential cooling with timescale τcool (nuisance, bounded by LMXB constraints), feeding η(T).
0.3 Crust elasticity (minimal coupling that matters for μeff): adopt a linear elastic crust with shear modulus μshear(ρ) and yielding threshold σbreak; implement as an elastic back-reaction on magnetic stresses at the crust (magneto-elastic induction), allowing plastic “slip” when σ>σbreak via a capped effective viscosity (one nuisance parameter controlling slip rate).
0.4 Observational nuisance set (explicit): distance d, inclination i, beaming factor bX (pulsations), radio radiative efficiency εR, and accretion-rate red-noise parameters (amplitude Aṁ, spectral slope β) for torque/pulse-phase noise.

Step 1 — Replace parameterized closures with an explicit, validated interior→exterior mapping:
1.1 Forward model domains (3-region coupling):
  (I) Interior + crust induction: evolve B with Hall+resistive induction on a fixed GR background (Cowling), using stratification from the EOS family.
  (II) Elastic crust: magneto-elastic coupling via stress balance at the crustal lattice; track shear strain energy and enforce yield criterion.
  (III) Exterior magnetosphere: solve axisymmetric+non-axisymmetric (low-m) resistive force-free electrodynamics (RFFE) or force-free with a thin resistive layer at the surface.
1.2 Boundary conditions at the stellar surface (explicit): enforce continuity of normal B and tangential E; allow surface currents consistent with the crustal electric field from Hall+η. This defines the exterior solution uniquely; μeff(t) is extracted from the asymptotic ℓ=1 component of the exterior field (spherical-harmonic decomposition) at r ≫ R.
1.3 Disk truncation and pulsation condition without free functionals:
  • Compute magnetospheric pressure balance using the exterior field solution at the equatorial plane: rm(t) from B_ext(r,θ=π/2,t) via standard balance with ṁ(t). No free “magnetization functional”; only nuisance accretion noise model.
  • Pulsation visibility model: pulse fraction/harmonics predicted from channeling geometry using rm/R and μeff(t) plus inclination i and spot-colatitude (spot geometry nuisance with bounded prior). Coherence loss predicted from time variability in μeff(t) and rm(t) convolved with ṁ red-noise.
1.4 Jet proxy grounded in magnetosphere: use open magnetic flux Φopen(t) from the force-free solution and estimate jet power scaling Pjet ∝ Φopen^2 Ω^2 (with a single radiative efficiency εR nuisance). This ties radio-loudness to a physically computed exterior quantity rather than a flexible closure.
1.5 Validation of μeff(t) as non-artifact dominated:
  • Gauge tests: compute μeff(t) from multiple extraction radii and from vector-potential vs field-based harmonic extraction; require <3% discrepancy.
  • Boundary robustness: vary surface resistive-layer thickness and numerical resolution; require μeff(t) spectra stable within tolerance.

Step 2 — High-fidelity simulation library with non-ideal effects and controlled accretion forcing:
2.1 Design of experiments (DoE): Latin hypercube over {EOS params} × {Qi,fη,fHall,σbreak} × {initial poloidal fraction, total B energy, rotation rate fixed to AMXP-like spins}.
2.2 Accretion forcing model (minimal but explicit): represent accretion as time-dependent surface mass loading and equatorial compression that modifies outer boundary conditions for induction (flux burial tendency) while keeping total accreted mass ΔM fixed per run; drive ṁ(t) with red-noise (Aṁ,β) matched to observed LMXB variability.
2.3 Outputs stored per run (for inference and identifiability):
  • μeff(t) time series and power spectrum Sμ(f)
  • Φopen(t), rm(t), torque N(t)
  • Mode content of internal B (m-spectrum) and toroidal fraction Etor/Eb
  • Crustal strain energy and yield events (predicting intermittency)

Step 3 — Reduced-order model (ROM) and adjoint-ready operator with hard constraints:
3.1 Structure-preserving ROM for magneto-thermal induction (Hall+η):
  • State vector: coefficients of divergence-free basis for B (constructed from vector potential A with constrained POD) + low-dimensional temperature state T(t).
  • Integrator: energy-stable IMEX scheme (implicit resistive term, explicit Hall term) preserving ∇·B=0 by construction.
  • Non-axisymmetric content: retain explicit low-m subspace (m=1–4) to capture Tayler-dominated structure; enforce selection-rule tracking (e.g., m=2 growth) via basis design.
3.2 Coupled exterior fast-solver surrogate: train a constrained surrogate mapping surface B and E to {μeff,Φopen} using a reduced force-free solver basis, but benchmark against full RFFE solutions; enforce Maxwell constraints at the boundary.
3.3 Discrete adjoint: implement adjoints for the ROM + exterior surrogate to compute ∂(log L)/∂(EOS params) and ∂/∂(nuisance) efficiently.
3.4 Success tolerance targets (pre-registered): ROM must reproduce held-out high-fidelity runs to
  • onset time of instability within 10%
  • μeff(t) RMS within 10% and dominant spectral slope within Δα=0.2
  • Φopen(t) mean within 15%

Step 4 — Observational likelihoods tied to explicit forward quantities:
4.1 AMXP timing likelihood:
  • Data: pulse fraction vs LX, harmonic ratios, phase residuals; torque-noise spectra when available.
  • Model: generate synthetic pulse trains using μeff(t), rm(t), i, spot geometry; compare via summary statistics (coherence time, phase-noise PSD, luminosity dependence of pulse fraction).
4.2 Radio/X-ray jet likelihood:
  • Data: quasi-simultaneous radio fluxes/spectra and X-ray luminosities; include radio-bright AMXPs (e.g., IGR J17591-2342-like leverage points).
  • Model: predict radio luminosity LR(t)=εR Pjet(t) with absorption/distance nuisance; compare via radio/X-ray plane trajectories and spectral index constraints.
4.3 RMSP endpoint likelihood:
  • Data: P, Pdot (Shklovskii-corrected), binary parameters.
  • Model: evolve post-accretion cooling T(t) and induction to late times to predict distribution of μeff,late; compare to inferred dipole moments with selection modeling (radio detectability vs B,P).
4.4 Companion information integration (bounded, not full population synthesis): use companion type to set priors on duty cycle and ṁ noise hyperparameters (Aṁ,β, τcool ranges), not to forward-evolve binaries.

Step 5 — Formal identifiability and degeneracy control (mandatory):
5.1 Fisher/adjoint sensitivity matrices: compute Sij=∂Oi/∂θj for observables O={Sμ(f) slopes/amplitudes, rm variability metrics, LR/LX trends, RMSP μlate} and parameters θ={EOS nodes, Qi,fη,fHall,σbreak,d,i,bX,εR,Aṁ,β}. Provide density-band attribution by mapping EOS perturbations to changes in ρ(r) regions that dominate ωA(r) and Hall timescale.
5.2 Null and alternative models (pre-registered):
  • Null A (fixed EOS, flexible emission/jet): allow εR,bX,spot geometry, Aṁ,β to vary; test whether it can reproduce joint AMXP+radio+RMSP constraints without changing EOS.
  • Null B (ideal-MHD only): remove Hall+η(T); demonstrate misfit to observed variability timescales or required μeff(t) spectra.
  • Alternative microphysics correlation test: allow Qi to correlate with EOS stiffness; quantify posterior degeneracy and show which observables break it (e.g., Hall-driven spectral transfer vs EOS-driven ωA shifts).
5.3 Sample-size requirement: perform simulation-based power analysis (synthetic catalogs) to determine Nsystems needed to constrain at least one EOS stiffness combination at target precision (e.g., 1σ width on pressure node P(2–3ρsat) < 30%), under realistic nuisance/systematic priors.

Step 6 — Deliverables and decision gates:
6.1 Gate 1 (forward-model credibility): demonstrate μeff(t) extraction robustness and ROM fidelity on held-out runs meeting tolerance targets.
6.2 Gate 2 (identifiability): pass null-model rejection on synthetic data at ≥95% (EOS-varying model preferred over fixed-EOS flexible-closure) and show at least one EOS density band is practically identifiable (condition number threshold on Fisher matrix).
6.3 Gate 3 (real-data pilot): apply to a small, high-quality subset (AMXPs with good timing + at least one radio-bright case + a matched RMSP set) and report whether EOS posteriors are informative or remain prior-dominated; if prior-dominated, report as falsification/limitation rather than overfitting closures.
Feasibility:
Addresses critique (i) closure/μeff mapping: The revised plan replaces free “magnetosphere/jet functionals” with an explicit, matched model: Hall+resistive induction in the crust provides surface E and B; a resistive/force-free exterior computes the open flux and the ℓ=1 multipole, defining μeff(t) uniquely and allowing gauge/boundary artifact tests (multi-radius extraction, resistive-layer thickness variation). Disk truncation rm(t) is computed directly from the exterior field rather than assumed.

Addresses critique (ii) microphysics confounding: Hall drift and η(T,Qi) are included as leading non-ideal terms with bounded nuisance parameters, plus a minimal thermal model informed by outburst/cooling. This allows explicit degeneracy tests between EOS stiffness and transport (including correlated priors), rather than collapsing them into an uncontrolled “conductivity proxy.” Crustal elasticity/yield provides a physically motivated intermittency channel that can imprint distinct features in μeff(t) spectra, aiding separation from EOS effects.

Addresses critique (iii) inference-grade fidelity: High-fidelity runs include the necessary non-ideal physics and explicit surface-to-magnetosphere matching, targeting the actual quantity used in inference (μeff and Φopen). The ROM is constrained (∇·B=0 by construction; IMEX stability; low-m content retained) and benchmarked with pre-registered tolerances, making it suitable for adjoint-based inversion.

Addresses critique (iv) observational systematics and identifiability: The plan introduces a formal Fisher/adjoint sensitivity program, explicit nuisance parameters (d,i,beaming, εR, ṁ red-noise), and null models that allow closures to vary while EOS is held fixed. This directly tests whether EOS information is genuinely required by the joint dataset. Sample-size requirements are pre-registered via simulation-based power analyses, and success metrics are quantitative (ROM errors, null rejection, identifiable density band). Radio-bright AMXPs (as in the empirical class exemplified by unusually radio-luminous accreting millisecond pulsars) provide leverage on Φopen-based jet power, while Tayler-driven non-axisymmetric evolution (supported by polytropic-instability simulations) provides a concrete internal mechanism whose observable imprint is μeff(t) variability and mode content.

Concept-chain coherence (LMXB→AMXP→RMSP): The same interior-to-exterior operator predicts (a) when magnetospheric channeling yields AMXP pulsations, (b) when open flux yields radio-loud compact jets during outburst, and (c) the late-time dipole distribution observed in RMSPs after accretion ends. Companion information is used only to constrain accretion/cooling priors, avoiding full population evolution while remaining physically grounded.
Critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and technically mature proposal that directly confronts prior identifiability criticisms rather than deflecting them. The engineering plan is detailed and largely credible, especially the explicit interior-to-exterior matching, μ_eff(t) extraction tests, and pre-registered ROM fidelity tolerances. The logical chain linking EOS-dependent stratification to Alfvén spectra, Tayler instability saturation, and observable magnetospheric variability is physically well motivated, though it remains contingent on the assumption that low-m non-axisymmetric evolution survives the combined effects of accretion forcing and crustal yielding at amplitudes detectable in current AMXP datasets. Evidence grounding is strong: the proposal stays within neutron-star MHD, crustal physics, and observational timing/radio diagnostics without conceptual drift. Minor deductions arise from the ambitious scope: the force-free exterior plus non-axisymmetric Hall-MHD coupling and elastic yielding may push computational feasibility and calibration risk, and the jet proxy (P_jet ∝ Φ_open^2 Ω^2) remains an approximate scaling rather than a first-principles jet solution. Overall, however, the rationale is deep, original, and directly addresses a known bottleneck in EOS inference from accreting millisecond systems.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that neutron-star radius constraints from binary neutron-star (BNS) mergers can be measurably sharpened (quantified as a reduction in the 68% credible interval width ΔR68 for R1.4) by a coherent joint framework that (i) uses inspiral information (chirp mass and tidal deformability) and (ii) adds post-merger remnant/disk information that is sensitive to EOS stiffness, while (iii) maintaining mathematical well-posedness by fixing a parameterized finite-temperature EOS per simulation (rather than enforcing any on-the-fly EOS projection during GRMHD evolution). The key mechanism is not a deterministic map Λ→Mdisk, but a statistically calibratable dependence of post-merger outcomes on a small set of stiffness proxies that simultaneously control (a) the inspiral tidal response (Λ, k2) and (b) the threshold for prompt collapse and the amount of angular momentum available to circularize into a torus. Concretely, for fixed binary intrinsic parameters (Mchirp, q, spins), EOS parameters shift the remnant’s maximum supported mass and compactness, thereby shifting the prompt-collapse boundary and the distribution of disk mass. Even when microphysics (neutrino cooling, turbulent angular-momentum transport, magnetic-field amplification) adds scatter, the prompt-collapse/no-collapse classification and the disk/ejecta mass scale retain informative, monotonic trends with EOS stiffness proxies that correlate with R1.4. By explicitly modeling this scatter via simulation-calibrated discrepancy terms within a hierarchical Bayesian inference, and by emulating the simulation outputs with reduced-order surrogates (rather than altering PDE closure), we can robustly propagate inspiral constraints (Λ and masses) to radius while marginalizing astrophysical and numerical systematics, yielding tighter and defensible EOS/radius posteriors than inspiral-only analyses.
Plan:
Step 1 — Define a mathematically well-posed finite-temperature EOS family (fixed parameters per run):
1.1 Parameterize the cold EOS with a piecewise-polytrope (PP) or spectral representation consistent with chiral EFT at low density, joined at fixed transition densities (e.g., {ρ1,ρ2,ρ3} in units of ρsat) with free polytropic indices/pressures {Γi or Pi}. Impose hard constraints: causality (cs≤c), thermodynamic stability (∂p/∂ρ>0), maximum mass Mmax≥2.0 M⊙ (to accommodate heavy pulsars), and continuity of p(ρ) and ε(ρ).
1.2 Extend to finite temperature using a standard additive thermal component with fixed Γth per simulation, p(ρ,ε)=pcold(ρ)+pth where pth=(Γth−1)ρ(ε−εcold(ρ)). Treat Γth as a calibrated nuisance hyperparameter (or a small discrete set, e.g., 1.5–2.0) rather than changing it dynamically.
1.3 Include composition/electron fraction in a controlled way: adopt a minimal Ye(ρ,T) prescription (e.g., beta-equilibrium for the cold part plus an approximate neutrino-leakage-based evolution during merger), and introduce a small number of “microphysics knobs” per simulation (e.g., neutrino leakage strength scaling fν and effective viscosity/alpha parameter αvisc) to capture uncertainty in cooling and angular-momentum transport.
1.4 For each EOS draw, compute TOV sequences and tidal deformabilities: M–R curve, Λ(M), k2(M), and derived proxies (R1.4, Λ1.4, compactness C1.4). Calibrate priors with multimessenger constraints including NICER J0740+6620 radii and GW constraints; maintain separate PP and speed-of-sound-informed priors at the level of EOS sampling (as in Asset 1), but always compile to the fixed finite-T closure above per simulation.

Step 2 — Design of experiments (DoE) and simulation campaign with explicit runtime budget:
2.1 Define intrinsic binary parameter space: sample (Mchirp, q) centered on observed BNS distributions; include aligned spins with |χ| up to a conservative BNS prior (e.g., 0–0.05 for typical systems; optionally extend to 0.1 for robustness). Use a Latin hypercube design over {EOS parameters, Mchirp, q, χ1, χ2, Γth, fν, αvisc}.
2.2 Simulation tiers to manage cost:
  Tier A (exploratory): GRHD + approximate thermal EOS + leakage (coarser resolution) to map prompt-collapse boundary and rough disk-mass scaling across a broad EOS set.
  Tier B (production): higher-resolution GRMHD with neutrino leakage (or M1 if available) on a reduced set chosen by active learning to resolve the Λ–outcome gradients; include MRI-aware resolution targets.
  Tier C (validation): a small “gold set” of EOS/binaries run with (i) higher resolution, (ii) alternative neutrino treatment (leakage vs M1), and (iii) at least one independent code for cross-code comparison.
2.3 Runtime budget specification (proposal-level): commit to N_A ~ O(50–100) Tier-A runs, N_B ~ O(20–40) Tier-B runs, and N_C ~ O(6–12) Tier-C runs, with wall-clock estimates per run based on available allocation; adjust N adaptively using surrogate-driven acquisition (Step 3.3).

Step 3 — Extract robust post-merger targets and build reduced-order surrogates for outputs (not for EOS closure):
3.1 Define simulation outputs y with direct physical meaning and observable connections:
  y1: prompt-collapse indicator (binary classification) and collapse time tcoll (if delayed collapse).
  y2: disk/torus baryonic mass Mdisk at a standard post-merger time (e.g., 10–20 ms after merger or after BH formation).
  y3: dynamical ejecta mass Mej,dyn and characteristic velocity vej (where reliably extracted).
  y4 (optional): remnant lifetime category (HMNS/SMNS/BH) and GW post-merger spectral proxy if within bandwidth assumptions.
3.2 Build emulators/surrogates y≈S(x) with x={Mchirp,q,χ1,χ2,EOS params,Γth,fν,αvisc}. Use Gaussian-process regression or neural surrogates with uncertainty quantification; for the collapse classifier use probabilistic classification (e.g., GP classification).
3.3 Include a model-discrepancy layer: represent unresolved physics and numerical error by additive and/or multiplicative discrepancy terms δy with hyperpriors informed by Tier-C cross-code/resolution comparisons (Step 5). This is central: the surrogate returns both mean predictions and predictive uncertainty that is carried into inference.
3.4 Active learning loop: iteratively add Tier-B simulations where surrogate uncertainty is highest in regions supported by GW posteriors (focusing compute where it most impacts ΔR68).

Step 4 — Hierarchical Bayesian inference combining inspiral and post-merger information with explicit nuisance/systematics:
4.1 Inspiral likelihood: use GW posterior samples or likelihood approximants for (Mchirp,q,χeff,Λ̃) with known measurement properties (Asset 2 indicates chirp-mass bias is negligible at ~10−3 M⊙; incorporate this as a tight calibration prior).
4.2 Post-merger “torus observables” and likelihood models (two realistic entry points):
  (A) Kilonova-informed ejecta/disk scale: use EM-inferred ejecta mass and velocity (from light-curve fits) with a systematic prior capturing radiative-transfer/opacity/viewing-angle uncertainty; map to disk mass via a phenomenological relation with nuisance parameters (e.g., fraction of disk unbound fw with wide prior). Likelihood: p(EM data | Mej,vej,fw,κ,θview,…) × p(Mej,vej | x, δy).
  (B) Collapse/no-collapse constraints: if a short-lived remnant is inferred (or if prompt-collapse is disfavored) from EM/GW considerations, encode as a likelihood on y1/tcoll with conservative classification error.
4.3 Full hierarchical model:
  p(EOS params, microphysics | GW, EM) ∝ p(GW | Mchirp,q,χ,Λ̃(EOS)) × p(EM | S(x)+δy, nuisance) × p(EOS params | nuclear+NICER priors) × p(microphysics,nuisance) × p(δy hyperparams).
4.4 Output target: posterior on R1.4 and R(M) at relevant masses, plus Bayes factors for EOS stiffness classes. Primary metric: reduction in ΔR68(R1.4) relative to inspiral-only baseline under identical priors.

Step 5 — Validation and robustness program (explicitly addressing numerical/microphysics sensitivity):
5.1 Resolution/MRI criteria: demonstrate convergence of Mdisk and tcoll with at least two resolutions; for GRMHD runs, report standard MRI resolvability metrics (e.g., quality factors Qθ,Qφ) in the disk and show whether results are in the asymptotic regime or incorporate a calibrated αvisc nuisance when not.
5.2 Neutrino treatment sensitivity: on the Tier-C set, compare leakage vs (if feasible) M1 transport impact on Mdisk, Ye-sensitive ejecta, and collapse time; encode differences into discrepancy hyperpriors.
5.3 Cross-code comparison: run the Tier-C set with an independent NR/GRMHD code or an established community benchmark configuration; quantify inter-code scatter in y and propagate as δy.
5.4 External consistency checks: verify that inferred R1.4 posteriors are consistent with NICER J0740+6620-informed constraints and with GW170817/GW190425 bounds (Asset 1), and test posterior predictive checks on EM observables.

Step 6 — Deliverables:
6.1 Publicly documented EOS parameterization and prior constraints (including causality and Mmax filters).
6.2 A validated surrogate package S(x) with uncertainty quantification and discrepancy calibration.
6.3 An end-to-end inference pipeline producing radius posteriors with transparent systematics and the ΔR68 improvement metric.
Feasibility:
Well-posedness and thermodynamic consistency: The closure is a standard parameterized finite-T EOS (cold PP/spectral + thermal Γth), with parameters fixed per simulation. This avoids ill-posed “on-the-fly projection” that could violate the first law or alter characteristic structure during evolution. Causality/stability are enforced at the EOS construction stage, and TOV/Λ consistency is guaranteed by design.

Mechanistic plausibility without overstated determinism: The proposal does not assume Λ uniquely determines the torus mass. Instead, it treats post-merger outcomes (prompt-collapse boundary, disk mass) as noisy but informative functions of intrinsic binary parameters and EOS stiffness proxies that also control R1.4/Λ. This is consistent with the empirical picture that disk formation depends on mass ratio, total mass vs threshold mass, and angular momentum redistribution (Assets 3–4), while inspiral Λ provides complementary stiffness information (Asset 1).

Realistic observables and explicit systematics: The incorporated post-merger constraints are limited to observables with plausible near-term access—kilonova-inferred ejecta properties and coarse collapse/no-collapse information—paired with conservative likelihoods and nuisance parameters (opacity/viewing angle/jet physics; disk-to-ejecta conversion). Model discrepancy is not hand-waved: it is encoded as hyperparameters calibrated by resolution studies, neutrino-treatment comparisons, and cross-code scatter, then marginalized in the hierarchical inference.

Computational credibility: The compute plan is explicitly tiered and DoE-driven (Latin hypercube + active learning). Reduced-order surrogates accelerate inference by emulating simulation outputs rather than modifying PDE closures, matching established practice and directly addressing reviewer concerns about cost and numerical ill-posedness.

Validation to reviewer standards: A concrete robustness program is included—resolution/MRI quality metrics, microphysics sensitivity (leakage vs M1 where feasible), and cross-code comparisons on a gold set—so that the learned Λ–post-merger correlations are demonstrably not artifacts of numerics or a single microphysics choice.

Quantified success criterion: The proposal commits to a primary performance metric (ΔR68 reduction for R1.4 relative to inspiral-only) and will report posterior predictive checks and calibration diagnostics to demonstrate that any radius improvement is statistically supported rather than driven by unmodeled systematics.
Critique: This is a technically mature and unusually well-scaffolded proposal. The engineering plan is credible, tiered, and explicitly cost-aware, and the insistence on mathematical well-posedness (fixed EOS closure, no on-the-fly projection) directly addresses a known failure mode in post-merger inference. The logical chain from EOS stiffness → threshold mass/prompt collapse → disk mass → EM observables → improved radius posteriors is articulated with appropriate caution and explicit stochastic modeling rather than unjustified determinism. Minor score deductions arise from residual risk: (i) the assumed monotonicity of disk-mass and collapse indicators with stiffness proxies may be partially obscured by angular-momentum transport and neutrino physics even after discrepancy modeling, and (ii) the achievable ΔR68 improvement is not forecast with quantitative mock-data studies, leaving some uncertainty about effect size under realistic EM errors.

Hypothesis:
Fast neutrino flavor conversions (FFCs) in post–neutron-star-merger disks produce a *direction-dependent* suppression of effective charged-current νe (and/or enhancement of ̅νe) absorption that shifts the freeze-out electron fraction Ye in disk-wind ejecta in a way that is not reproducible by composition-independent opacity/heating rescalings. The key mechanism is that ELN-crossing–triggered flavor equilibration acts *only* in regions where the reconstructed electron-lepton-number angular distribution G(μ)≡fνe(μ)−f̅νe(μ) changes sign; this produces a latitude-dependent Ye redistribution (high-latitude outflows become more neutron rich than predicted by flavor-blind M1), yielding (i) a more strongly bimodal lanthanide fraction between polar and equatorial ejecta components, (ii) a constrained change in actinide/lanthanide heating partition (including fission recycling contributions), and (iii) an observable, time-localized signature in AT 2023vfi’s multi-band color evolution and late-time IR slope that survives marginalization over ejecta mass/velocity morphology.

We overcome the reviewers’ identifiability and well-posedness concerns by replacing the previously vague “geometry proxies + learned correction” with a mathematically explicit, realizable *ELN-reconstruction-and-closure pipeline* that (a) reconstructs a provably positive angular distribution consistent with the first two moments, (b) derives a sufficient (and, in a defined class, necessary) ELN-crossing criterion from those reconstructed distributions plus controlled uncertainty bounds, and (c) modifies interaction rates—not the transport hyperbolic structure—through a lepton-number–conserving source-term map calibrated to Boltzmann/Monte Carlo snapshots with known angular ELN structure. The closure is thus engineering-resolved: transport remains a standard realizable M1 system (guaranteeing hyperbolicity/causality), while flavor physics enters through a constrained, calibration-anchored mapping from moments → ELN crossing probability → rate modifiers → Ye evolution → r-process yields → kilonova observables.
Plan:
Step 0 (Pre-registration and scope lock):
0.1 Pre-register (before inference) the exact flavor-aware parameterization, the minimal set of “flavor-unique” observables, and the degeneracy tests (SBC/PPC) described in Step 4. Freeze all prior families (not hyperparameters) to prevent Bayes-factor drift.

Step 1 (AT 2023vfi observational dataset and forward-model targets):
1.1 Assemble AT 2023vfi photometry and spectra (including JWST if available) and homogenize to a forward-modeling data vector D={Fν(tk), colors Cij(tk), selected spectral pseudo-EWs / continuum slopes}. Define three pre-registered summary observables that we will treat as “flavor-unique targets”:
  O1: time of maximum of near-IR color index (e.g., (F200W−F444W) or closest bands) relative to bolometric peak (Δtcolor),
  O2: curvature (“kink statistic”) in color evolution during days ~3–10 (second-derivative sign change in a spline fit with fixed knots),
  O3: late-time (>10–15 d) IR spectral slope / effective temperature decay index, which is sensitive to heating partition and thermalization.
(These are chosen because pure morphology changes mainly shift diffusion times and peak luminosity, whereas a latitude-dependent Ye bimodality changes the time-evolving effective opacity and heating in a way that produces identifiable curvature and late-time slope changes.)

1.2 Build an ejecta background ensemble anchored to NR-informed priors: dynamical ejecta + disk wind with parameters θejecta={Mej,dyn, vej,dyn, Ye,dyn, Mej,wind, vej,wind, s_wind, geometry angles}. Constrain to match empirical lanthanide-rich mass scale (~0.02 M⊙ as suggested by AT 2023vfi modeling) and velocity ranges consistent with KN phenomenology.

Step 2 (Mathematically explicit ELN angular reconstruction from moments and crossing conditions):
We do not attempt to infer the full energy-angle distribution from moments; instead we reconstruct an *effective angular ELN distribution* G(μ) from νe and ̅νe moments using a realizable maximum-entropy (ME) ansatz with uncertainty bounds.

2.1 Input moments (per species) from M1 state: energy density E, flux vector F, and (optionally) number density N if tracked; otherwise use a spectral closure (Step 3.2) to map E↔N.
Define flux factor f≡|F|/E and μ as cosine w.r.t. local flux direction.

2.2 Reconstruct positive angular distributions via the ME/Minerbo family (realizable by construction):
For each species s∈{νe,̅νe}, define
  f_s(μ) = A_s exp( B_s μ ),   μ∈[−1,1]
with A_s, B_s chosen such that
  E_s ∝ ∫_{−1}^{1} f_s(μ) dμ,
  F_s ∝ ∫_{−1}^{1} μ f_s(μ) dμ.
This yields a unique mapping between (E_s,F_s) and (A_s,B_s) for 0≤f_s<1, and guarantees f_s(μ)≥0 (realizability/positivity).

2.3 Define the reconstructed ELN angular distribution:
  G(μ) = f_{νe}(μ) − f_{\barνe}(μ).
Crossing exists if ∃ μ such that G(μ)=0 with sign change.

2.4 Sufficient/forbidden crossing conditions from moments (guarantee logic):
Let r(μ)≡f_{νe}(μ)/f_{\barνe}(μ) = (A_{νe}/A_{\barνe}) exp[(B_{νe}−B_{\barνe})μ].
Because r(μ) is monotone in μ, any crossing of G(μ) can occur at most once in μ for this class.
A crossing exists iff min_μ r(μ) ≤ 1 ≤ max_μ r(μ).
Since μ∈[−1,1], this is equivalent to:
  r(−1) ≤ 1 ≤ r(+1)   or   r(+1) ≤ 1 ≤ r(−1).
We compute r(±1) explicitly from (A_s,B_s) and thus from moments. Therefore, within the ME class, the moment set provides a *necessary and sufficient* crossing test.

2.5 Robustness to reconstruction error (uncertainty bounds):
We bracket the ME reconstruction by a two-parameter “tilted ME” family that preserves positivity:
  f_s(μ) = A_s exp(B_s μ + C_s μ^2), with C_s ∈ [Cmin,Cmax] chosen so that the implied Eddington factor χ stays within the realizable interval (Minerbo bounds). This generates an interval for r(±1) and thus a crossing probability p_cross∈[0,1]. We propagate p_cross into rate modifiers (Step 3) so that classification uncertainty becomes a quantified model component rather than an uncontrolled misclassification risk.

Step 3 (Explicit flavor-to-rate map with detailed balance and energy dependence):
We treat FFCs as rapid compared to weak interaction times in identified p_cross>0 regions, driving partial flavor equilibration. We compress the linear stability outputs into a bounded, calibration-anchored suppression factor acting on charged-current rates.

3.1 Linear fast-limit stability module (offline):
For each local state x={ρ,T,Ye,Eνe,Fνe,E\barνe,F\barνe, (optional) spectral temperatures Tνe,T\barνe }, compute the fast-mode growth rate κ_fast from the dispersion relation in the “fast” QKE limit using the reconstructed G(μ) as the angular input. Output diagnostics:
  (i) p_cross(x) from Step 2,
  (ii) κ_fast(x),
  (iii) a mixing efficiency proxy m(x)=1−exp[−α κ_fast τ_adv], where τ_adv is a local advection/expansion timescale from the outflow model and α is a calibration constant.

3.2 Energy dependence and spectra marginalization:
Adopt a pinched-spectrum parameterization for each species with parameters (⟨εν⟩,α_pin) and enforce consistency between E and number density N (if N not evolved) via:
  N_s = E_s / ⟨εν⟩_s.
We marginalize energy dependence of absorption by evaluating energy-weighted cross sections ⟨σ(ε)⟩ over the pinched spectra (pre-tabulated), so the rate map depends on (E_s,F_s,⟨εν⟩_s,α_pin).

3.3 Rate-modifier functional form (bounded + detailed-balance consistent):
Define baseline charged-current absorption/emission rates λ^{0}_{νe n→pe−}, λ^{0}_{\barνe p→ne+} from standard microphysics using the local spectra.
We apply flavor via multiplicative modifiers:
  λ_{νe} = λ^{0}_{νe} [1 − S(x)],
  λ_{\barνe} = λ^{0}_{\barνe} [1 + \bar S(x)]
with
  S(x) = s_max · p_cross(x) · m(x),
  \bar S(x) = \bar s_max · p_cross(x) · m(x),
and bounds 0≤S≤s_max<1, 0≤\bar S≤\bar s_max set by calibration.

Detailed balance constraint: we enforce that the modified net source terms satisfy equilibrium at the same chemical potentials when p_cross→0, and we do not modify neutral-current processes. In practice, we implement modification at the level of effective νe and ̅νe occupation numbers entering both absorption and emission kernels so that Kirchhoff’s law holds; the multiplicative form above is the summary, while the implementation modifies both forward/backward kernels consistently.

3.4 Lepton-number conservation in the coupled source terms:
Update Ye through
  dYe/dt = (Γ_{νe} − Γ_{\barνe}) / n_b,
with Γ computed from modified rates. Enforce discrete conservation by updating matter and neutrino moments with equal-and-opposite lepton-number exchange in the operator-split source step (to solver tolerance). This is an algorithmic constraint checked in Step 5.

3.5 Transport/closure well-posedness (responding to hyperbolicity critique):
We keep the *transport closure* as standard realizable M1 (Minerbo Eddington tensor):
  P_ij = χ E n_i n_j + (1−χ)E δ_ij/2,
  χ=χ(f) in the Minerbo form.
Thus hyperbolicity/causality of the homogeneous moment system is unchanged (characteristic speeds bounded by c). Flavor enters only through source terms (rates), not through ΔP_ij. This directly resolves the “proof of characteristic-speed bounds for modified closure” requirement by construction.
(If the solicitation explicitly requires a ΔP_ij term, we include a *strictly realizable* anisotropy correction that preserves Minerbo bounds: define χ_eff = χ + δχ with δχ = ε_p p_cross m (1−χ) and clamp χ_eff to [1/3,1]. Then set ΔP_ij = (χ_eff−χ)E(n_i n_j−δ_ij/3). Realizability follows from χ_eff bounds; hyperbolicity is verified numerically via eigenvalue checks in Step 5. However, the default implementation avoids altering transport and modifies only rates.)

Step 4 (Inference design to control degeneracy and ensure identifiability):
4.1 Parameterization for inference:
Global parameters: θglobal={s_max,\bar s_max, α (mixing-timescale factor), spectral pinching priors, nuclear heating nuisance parameters within evaluated nuclear model spread}.
Ejecta parameters: θejecta with tight NR-informed priors and explicit geometry controls (opening angles, two-component mass partition).
Opacity/heating: use composition-dependent opacities from the r-process network; include a minimal thermalization-efficiency parameterization with priors from existing KN studies.

4.2 Degeneracy study plan (mandatory):
(i) Simulation-Based Calibration (SBC): generate mock datasets from known θ including both FFC-on and FFC-off; run full inference; verify rank statistics for s_max and α are uniform and that Bayes factor recovers ground truth.
(ii) Posterior Predictive Checks (PPC): evaluate whether the inferred model reproduces O1–O3 and full lightcurve residual structure; require that improvements are not confined to a single band/epoch.
(iii) Confounder ablations: repeat inference with (a) widened opacity priors, (b) alternative nuclear heating models (incl. actinide-fission variance), (c) flexible morphology (additional velocity component). The FFC Bayes factor must remain stable (pre-registered threshold) or the claim is rejected.

4.3 Model comparison:
Compute Z_on and Z_off evidences for FFC-on vs FFC-off with identical ejecta/opacity priors; report Bayes factor K=Z_on/Z_off with uncertainty from nested sampling diagnostics.

Step 5 (Controlled validation against known angular ELN structure; quantifying Ye-freeze-out error):
5.1 Controlled snapshot suite (mandatory anchor):
Commit to at least one controlled dataset of post-merger-disk neutrino transport solutions with available angular distributions (Boltzmann or Monte Carlo). If collaboration/data access is required, secure an MoU and list the dataset(s) explicitly in the management plan.

5.2 Closure/reconstruction validation metrics:
For each snapshot cell/trajectory:
  (i) Compare reconstructed f_s(μ) against the true angular distribution projected onto μ: quantify KL divergence and errors in sign structure of G(μ).
  (ii) Crossing classification: compute precision/recall for ELN crossing; also compute calibrated p_cross reliability diagrams.
  (iii) Ye freeze-out error: evolve a one-zone or trajectory-based outflow using (a) true angle-dependent rates from the snapshot and (b) moment-reconstructed + flavor-modified rates. Compare ΔYe at freeze-out and resulting lanthanide fraction X_La.
Acceptance criteria (pre-registered): median |ΔYe| below a set threshold (e.g., 0.02) for trajectories dominating mass outflow; quantify tail risk.

5.3 Numerical well-posedness and stiffness:
Verify (a) realizability: E≥0 and |F|≤E always; (b) causality: characteristic speeds from the homogeneous M1 system ≤c (already guaranteed) and, if χ_eff is used, numerically check eigenvalues across state-space; (c) source-term stability: implicit/IMEX integration for stiff weak rates with lepton-number conservation error <10^{-8} per step (or solver tolerance).

Step 6 (End-to-end production: outflow → network → radiative transfer → AT 2023vfi constraints):
6.1 Evolve axisymmetric disk-wind trajectories with the flavor-modified rates to produce Ye(θ), s(θ), τexp(θ).
6.2 Run a full r-process network including fission recycling and actinide production to produce abundances, heating rates, and opacities; explicitly track nuclides highlighted in AT 2023vfi-like modeling (e.g., 222Rn, 223–225Ra, 225Ac) as diagnostic outputs.
6.3 Radiative transfer: generate synthetic lightcurves/spectra; compute O1–O3 and full data likelihood for inference.

Step 7 (Falsification and EOS implications):
7.1 Falsification: if data prefer FFC-on, they must also prefer the predicted *latitude-induced bimodality* signature—tested by enforcing a single-Ye component (no angular variation) while allowing heating/opacity freedom. If Bayes factor collapses, the signal is not flavor-specific.
7.2 EOS/remnant lifetime coupling: propagate posterior shifts in required disk-wind mass and Ye distribution into constraints on remnant lifetime/EOS stiffness under priors consistent with causality and maximum NS mass; quantify how flavor-aware Ye changes inferred ejecta partition relative to flavor-blind models.
Feasibility:
Addressing the four mandatory reviewer demands explicitly:

(1) Explicit realizable ELN reconstruction + crossing guarantees: We provide a concrete, positive maximum-entropy angular ansatz f_s(μ)=A_s exp(B_s μ) uniquely determined by (E_s,F_s). Within this class, an ELN crossing exists iff r(−1)≤1≤r(+1) (or vice versa), where r(μ)=fνe/f\barνe is monotone; this yields a necessary-and-sufficient crossing criterion, not an ad hoc “geometry proxy.” We further bracket reconstruction uncertainty with a strictly positive tilted family and propagate it as a crossing probability p_cross.

(2) Closure/ΔP_ij realizability, hyperbolicity, characteristic speeds: The proposal is re-engineered so that transport remains standard realizable M1 (Minerbo), which is known to be hyperbolic and causal (|characteristic speeds|≤c) under the usual realizability constraints E≥0 and |F|≤E. Flavor physics is injected through lepton-number–conserving source-term modifications to weak rates, avoiding unproven alterations of the hyperbolic flux Jacobian. If a ΔP_ij is required, we specify ΔP_ij=(χ_eff−χ)E(n_i n_j−δ_ij/3) with χ_eff clamped to [1/3,1], guaranteeing realizability; hyperbolicity is then verified by explicit eigenvalue checks across the sampled state space.

(3) Linear-stability compression into rate modifiers with energy dependence + calibration: We define the angular input to stability analysis as the reconstructed ELN distribution G(μ). We compute κ_fast in the fast limit and compress it into a bounded mixing efficiency m(x)=1−exp(−α κ_fast τ_adv). Rate modifiers are S(x)=s_max p_cross m and \bar S(x)=\bar s_max p_cross m, implemented at the kernel level to preserve detailed balance. Energy dependence is handled by pre-tabulated energy-averaged cross sections under a pinched-spectrum model, tying modifiers to spectral parameters rather than ignoring spectra. We calibrate (s_max,\bar s_max,α) against at least one controlled Boltzmann/MC snapshot suite with known angular distributions, and validate on Ye freeze-out errors, not merely crossing maps.

(4) Identifiability in AT 2023vfi inference: We pre-register a minimal “flavor-unique” observable set (O1–O3) designed to be sensitive to time-dependent opacity/heating changes from an angular Ye bimodality rather than to global diffusion-time shifts. We execute a rigorous degeneracy program: SBC to demonstrate recoverability of flavor parameters; PPC to ensure improvements are not band/epoch artifacts; and confounder ablations (widened opacity/heating/morphology priors) to demonstrate Bayes factors are not prior-driven. The falsification test (single-Ye forced) ensures that any claimed detection depends on the *geometry-dependent* Ye imprint central to the hypothesis.

Grounding in literature assets: Asset 2 motivates the physical directionality (latitude dependence) and mechanism (νe suppression → neutron-richer outflow) that our reconstructed ELN-crossing pipeline targets; Asset 1 provides the empirical anchor (AT 2023vfi/GRB 230307A similarity to AT 2017gfo, lanthanide-rich mass scale ~0.02 M⊙, and actinide-sensitive heating diagnostics) that makes the end-to-end inference and actinide-yield outputs observationally meaningful. The revised plan is therefore both mechanistically faithful and mathematically specified to the level required for correctness, calibration, and falsifiability.
Critique: This is an unusually detailed and technically mature proposal that directly addresses prior identifiability, realizability, and hyperbolicity objections. The ELN reconstruction and crossing logic are mathematically explicit and appropriately scoped to what moment data can support, and the decision to confine flavor effects to lepton-number–conserving source terms is logically sound and well justified. The inference design is disciplined (pre-registration, SBC, ablations) and shows a strong awareness of degeneracy risks. Minor weaknesses remain: (i) the maximum-entropy angular family, while realizable, is still a restrictive class and may underrepresent multi-lobed angular structure seen in some Boltzmann solutions; (ii) the compression of fast-mode dynamics into a single mixing-efficiency scalar m(x) risks washing out regime-dependent behavior unless the calibration dataset is sufficiently diverse; and (iii) the claim that O1–O3 are 'flavor-unique' is plausible but not rigorously proven beyond controlled ablations. These issues are limitations of scope rather than logical flaws.

Hypothesis:
In the small subset of high-accretion LMXBs that occupy Z-source-like states yet still produce thermonuclear (type-I) bursts, a measurable, energy-dependent distortion of burst observables (hardness evolution, apparent emitting area/temperature tracks, and inter-band time lags) is produced by burst photons traversing a compact reprocessing layer located at the inner-disk wind base or circumbinary/excretion structure. The mechanism is explicitly time-dependent radiative transfer in a medium with Thomson optical depth τes ≲ 1 (to avoid erasing the burst rise), column NH ~ 10^22–10^24 cm−2, and density n ~ 10^12–10^14 cm−3, whose ionization parameter ξ(t)=L(t)/(nr^2) changes rapidly during the burst. During the rise, photoionization reduces low-energy opacity (soft X-rays ‘recover’), while Compton scattering induces a hard-tail redistribution and a path-length (arrival-time) distribution that generates measurable, energy-dependent lags at the ~10−4–10−1 s level depending on τes and radius r. 

This proposal addresses reviewer-identified limitations by (i) committing to a minimal, identifiable transfer model with an explicit time-delay kernel (a Green’s-function mixture over scattering order for a single-zone shell), (ii) pre-registering which data products break which degeneracies (time-resolved spectra constrain NH(t), ξ(t), kTe; lag spectra constrain τes and r through the delay kernel; external distance priors constrain intrinsic luminosity/area evolution; GR light bending is treated as a controlled systematic rather than a primary M/R lever), and (iii) narrowing the EOS deliverable: instead of claiming precise M/R constraints from Z-source bursts, we will quantify and reduce systematic bias in inferred burst energetics and radius-expansion (PRE) diagnostics (apparent radius, touchdown flux) induced by reprocessing. Where rotational waveform information exists (rare) or independent radius anchors are available, we will propagate the corrected burst observables to compactness posteriors; otherwise compactness enters as a weakly informative nuisance parameter with conservative priors.

The refined approach overcomes conventional phenomenological burst fitting limitations (e.g., blackbody + ad hoc varying NH) because it enforces: (1) photon-number conservation in scattering, (2) physically constrained energy redistribution (Klein–Nishina/thermal Compton kernel), (3) a causality-respecting time-delay kernel tied to geometry (r/c scaling and scattering order), and (4) rate-equation-limited ionization evolution, preventing arbitrarily fast opacity changes that can otherwise mimic area/temperature evolution. This converts burst hardness/lag signatures from ambiguous ‘spectral variability’ into a constrained inverse problem whose identifiability is pre-quantified via Fisher/SBC forecasts under NICER/Swift time resolution and counting statistics.
Plan:
A. Sample lock + expected yield (pre-registered)
1) Target list (primary): known/suspected Z-like or high-luminosity dipping LMXBs with reported thermonuclear bursts and/or strong evidence of burst-like events, and with available high time-resolution soft X-ray data:
   - Primary bursters with rich public burst archives (controls and method validation): 4U 1636–536, 4U 1728–34, Aql X-1 (atoll; establishes baseline with minimal reprocessing).
   - High-inclination / dipping systems with strong variable scattering/absorption (reprocessing archetypes; some are not canonical Z but are the closest empirical analogs for the proposed mechanism): GX 13+1 (IXPE polarimetric asset; dipping + polarization swings), and additional dipping bursters identifiable from MINBAR/NICER archives.
   - Z-source candidates with bursts are rare; we will include any with confirmed type-I bursts during the NICER era (explicitly enumerated after a MINBAR cross-match and literature audit). The proposal’s population claim is limited to ‘high-accretion and/or dipping LMXBs’, with Z-track diagnostics used when applicable.
2) Data sources and burst counts:
   - Build an a priori burst inventory by cross-matching MINBAR + NICER burst catalogs + Swift/XRT trigger lists, producing: (i) number of bursts per source, (ii) peak count rates in NICER (0.3–10 keV) and Swift/XRT (0.5–10 keV), (iii) availability of pre-burst persistent segments, (iv) overlap with IXPE windows (if any). Deliverable: a table with expected usable bursts (S/N and time resolution constraints) and a ‘minimum viable dataset’ threshold: ≥30 high-S/N bursts across ≥3 sources, with ≥10 in reprocessing-prone states (dipping/high hardness).
3) Contingency if IXPE absent:
   - Polarimetry becomes optional; the primary constraints come from spectra + lag spectra. If IXPE is unavailable, we (i) tighten geometric priors using dipping depth/ingress-egress times and persistent spectral diagnostics, and (ii) focus the deliverable on bias correction of burst energetics rather than geometric reconstruction.

B. Minimal transfer model (explicit) and forward simulator
4) Geometry (minimal, reviewer-mandated): single-zone spherical or quasi-spherical shell covering fraction fc around the burst emission region at radius r, thickness Δr=ηr with η fixed (e.g., 0.1) in the minimal model. Parameters: {τes, NH, r, fc, kTe, vturb (optional broadening), baseline ion fractions}. Rationale: the shell provides an analytically tractable time-delay kernel and avoids non-identifiable multi-zone freedom.
5) Time-delay kernel (explicit Green’s-function mixture):
   - Observed photon arrival-time distribution is modeled as
     p(Δt|E,t)= (1−fc)δ(Δt) + fc * Σ_{m=0}^{mmax} Pm(τes) Gm(Δt; r, kTe)
     where m is scattering order, Pm(τes)=e^{−τes} τes^m / m! (Poisson in thin/moderate regime), and Gm is the path-length distribution for m scatterings in a shell. Minimal choice:
     - G0(Δt)=δ(Δt) (unscattered within covered fraction treated as absorbed-only channel)
     - For m≥1, approximate Δt as Gamma-distributed with mean ⟨Δt⟩m = m * (ℓ/c), variance m*(ℓ/c)^2, with ℓ ≡ (r/ max(1,τes)) as an effective step length; this reproduces (i) linear growth of mean delay with scattering order and (ii) broadening with m. This kernel is validated against Monte Carlo radiative transfer for τes ≤ 1; if τes drifts above 1 in fits, we switch to a diffusion-kernel approximation and flag rise-time washing constraints (see below).
6) Energy redistribution per scattering (minimal): thermal Compton kernel with electron temperature kTe (few keV–tens of keV), implemented as a precomputed response matrix K(E→E′;kTe) that enforces detailed balance and conserves photon number in the scattering channel. For τes ≤ 1, truncate at mmax ~ 5 is sufficient; energy redistribution is applied m times (convolutional operator).
7) Absorption + ionization kinetics (explicit ODE constraint):
   - Absorption optical depth τabs(E,t)=NH(t)*σpe(E, x_i(t)) where x_i are ionic fractions.
   - Ion fractions evolve via stiff ODEs: dx_i/dt = Ii(ξ(t),T) − Ri(n,T)*x_i with ξ(t)=L(t)/(n r^2). L(t) is the intrinsic burst luminosity from the emission model (not the observed one), ensuring causality and eliminating arbitrary opacity changes. Recombination coefficients and photoionization rates are tabulated (e.g., XSTAR/Cloudy grids) and interpolated.
8) Rise-time preservation constraint (feasibility guardrail): impose a hard prior that the transfer function cannot smear the rise beyond what is observed. Operationally: require the modeled convolved rise time t_rise,model(E) ≤ t_rise,obs(E)+Δt_instr, which strongly penalizes τes and r combinations that would ‘wash out’ sub-second rises.

C. Intrinsic burst emission + GR treatment (realistic scope)
9) Intrinsic spectral model: time-dependent color-corrected blackbody or atmosphere grid (if available), with parameters {T(t), A(t)} (apparent emitting area evolution) and optional PRE phases.
10) GR light bending mapping (Schwarzschild) is included as a controlled systematic, not the primary inference driver:
   - Use a standard light-bending prescription for a uniform surface (or hotspot only if burst oscillations are detected) to map emitted intensity to observed flux. Compactness u=2GM/(Rc^2) is assigned a conservative prior informed by known NS mass bounds; unless oscillations/waveform information exist, u is treated as weakly constrained and marginalized. Deliverable is bias reduction on A(t), PRE diagnostics, and energetics after correcting for reprocessing.

D. Identifiability package (mandatory): forecasts + parameter recovery
11) Detectability simulations (NICER/Swift time resolution):
   - Generate synthetic bursts (rise ~0.5–2 s, decay ~5–20 s) with instrument response and Poisson noise.
   - Scan grid: τes ∈ [0,1], r ∈ [3×10^6, 3×10^9] cm, NH ∈ [10^22,10^24] cm−2, n ∈ [10^12,10^14] cm−3, fc ∈ [0.1,1].
   - Compute predicted (i) lag-vs-energy spectra using cross-correlation/phase lags between 0.5–1 keV and 3–8 keV bands, (ii) time-resolved hardness tracks, (iii) spectral residual patterns relative to pure blackbody.
   - Produce detection contours: minimum burst peak counts and bin sizes needed to detect lags of 0.1 ms, 1 ms, 10 ms, 0.1 s at ≥3σ. Deliverable: a figure/table mapping (τes,r) to detectable lag for NICER-like count rates.
12) Formal degeneracy analysis:
   - Fisher matrix on summary statistics {time-resolved spectral parameters, lag spectrum coefficients, rise-time constraints} to quantify parameter correlations among {A(t) hyperparameters, distance D (with priors), τes, r, NH(t0), n, fc, kTe}.
   - Simulation-based calibration (SBC): draw θ from priors, simulate datasets, refit, and verify rank statistics; report where posteriors are biased or non-identifiable.
   - Pre-register identifiability claims:
     * Lag spectrum primarily constrains (τes, r) through mean delay scaling ~ (τes r)/c in thin/moderate regime.
     * Soft-band (≤2 keV) time-dependent curvature constrains NH(t) and ξ(t) (hence n r^2).
     * High-energy tail curvature constrains kTe and scattering fraction fc.
     * Distance D and intrinsic area A(t) remain degenerate with absolute luminosity; broken only with external D priors (e.g., globular cluster membership or Gaia for counterparts where possible) or PRE touchdown assumptions in control sources.
13) Benchmark inference engines (mandatory):
   - Baseline hierarchical Bayesian forward model (HBM): explicit physical simulator + standard MCMC/NUTS for per-burst parameters with hierarchical priors across bursts (state-dependent τes/NH allowed).
   - Normalizing flow (NF) is optional and will be adopted only if it demonstrably improves efficiency without changing posterior content:
     * Benchmark metric: wall-clock per effective sample size and posterior agreement (KL divergence / SBC ranks) versus HBM on synthetic and real bursts.
     * If NF used, it is restricted to amortizing the likelihood or proposing parameters; the final reported posteriors are validated against the HBM on a representative subset.

E. Analysis workflow on real data
14) Data reduction:
   - NICER: apply standard screening, background estimation, deadtime correction; generate sub-second light curves around rise; adaptive bins in tail with minimum counts per bin.
   - Swift/XRT: simultaneous time-resolved spectra where available; cross-calibration constants.
15) Joint fitting per burst:
   - Fit time-resolved spectra + lag spectra simultaneously with the minimal transfer model.
   - Perform posterior predictive checks on: rise profile preservation, lag-energy shape, and spectral curvature evolution.
16) State dependence / ‘Z-like’ linkage (appropriately narrowed):
   - For sources with Z-track diagnostics (hardness–intensity/CD position), test whether inferred τes, NH, fc correlate with track position or persistent hardness.
   - For dipping sources, test whether inferred τes/NH are consistent with dip depth and (if available) polarization degree/angle changes (Asset 1) as an external consistency check.

F. Deliverables (realistic EOS/physics impact)
17) Primary deliverable: quantify and correct systematic bias in inferred burst energetics and apparent radius evolution caused by reprocessing. Provide corrected distributions of (i) burst fluence, (ii) peak flux, (iii) PRE touchdown flux (where applicable), (iv) apparent emitting area tracks.
18) Secondary deliverable: constraints on reprocessing medium: τes, r, NH(t), n via ξ(t), and covering fraction fc, and their dependence on accretion state.
19) Conditional EOS deliverable (only when justified): if bursts with oscillations or independent radius anchors exist in the sample, propagate corrected observables into compactness constraints; otherwise report compactness-marginalized corrections and explicitly state that spectroscopy+transfer alone does not yield competitive M/R for Z sources.
Feasibility:
1) Quantitative feasibility of lag/spectral signatures (addresses critique iii):
- Sub-second lags require compact radii. In the thin/moderate regime, the mean scattering delay scales approximately as ⟨Δt⟩ ~ (τes r)/c (up to O(1) geometric factors captured in the kernel). This implies:
  * r ~ 3×10^7 cm with τes~0.3 gives ⟨Δt⟩~0.3 ms;
  * r ~ 3×10^8 cm with τes~0.3 gives ⟨Δt⟩~3 ms;
  * r ~ 3×10^9 cm with τes~0.3 gives ⟨Δt⟩~30 ms.
These values are within NICER timing capability provided sufficient counts; the proposal therefore targets burst subsets with high peak count rates and uses frequency-domain lag estimation as well as time-domain CCF to optimize S/N.
- Rise-time washing sets an upper envelope on τes and r. Our hard rise-time preservation prior operationalizes this constraint, preventing the model from ‘explaining’ lags with optically thick diffusion that would contradict observed sharp rises.

2) Identifiability risk management (addresses critique i):
- We explicitly separate which observables constrain which parameter combinations and we will publish Fisher/SBC identifiability maps.
- Key degeneracy breaks:
  * (τes,r) are constrained by the lag kernel shape and scaling, largely independent of distance and intrinsic area.
  * (NH, ξ(t)) are constrained by soft-band curvature and its time evolution; the ODE kinetics prevent arbitrary NH(t) morphing.
  * (fc,kTe) are constrained by the relative strength/shape of the hard Comptonized component and the fraction of delayed photons.
- Remaining degeneracies (distance vs intrinsic area) are acknowledged and handled with external priors or by reporting distance-marginalized corrected observables. We do not claim that M/R is identifiable in generic Z-source bursts without oscillations.

3) Sample realism (addresses critique ii):
- The proposal no longer hinges on a large population of bona fide Z-source bursters. Instead, it targets a feasible dataset combining: (i) abundant atoll bursts for calibration and null tests, and (ii) a smaller set of high-accretion/dipping systems (including GX 13+1-like environments) where reprocessing is independently indicated (dips, hardness swings, polarization changes per Asset 1).
- A pre-study burst census (MINBAR+NICER+Swift) is an explicit first deliverable; success criteria are tied to ‘minimum viable dataset’ thresholds rather than optimistic population claims.

4) Method choice justification (addresses critique iv):
- A conventional hierarchical Bayesian forward model (HBM) is the baseline and will be used for final inference robustness.
- Normalizing flows are treated as an optional accelerator only after benchmarking; if they do not preserve calibrated posteriors (SBC), they will be dropped. This directly addresses concerns about unnecessary complexity and bias/variance obscuration.

5) EOS claim narrowing (addresses critique v):
- The revised claim is to reduce systematic error in burst-derived quantities (energetics, apparent radius/PRE diagnostics) by explicitly modeling reprocessing. Any EOS/compactness inference is conditional on the presence of additional information (oscillation waveforms or independent radius anchors). GR light bending is retained to ensure physically consistent mapping and to marginalize a known systematic, not to promise high-precision M/R from Z-source spectroscopy.

6) Grounding in literature assets (context chain coherence):
- Asset 1 motivates using dipping/polarization variability as an external indicator of scattering geometry and optical depth changes, supporting the existence of a variable reprocessing medium.
- Asset 2 motivates burst–persistent flux coupling and provides typical burst timescales/fluxes for detectability simulations.
- Asset 3 provides the GR light-bending mapping used to keep intrinsic emission physically consistent while remaining conservative about identifiability.
- Asset 4 motivates considering dense-cloud opacity and (optionally) pair processes, but we restrict pair opacity to a testable add-on only if the data require high-energy tails.

Overall, the revised project is structured as a defensible, simulation-validated inverse problem: minimal transfer physics + explicit delay kernel + formal identifiability forecasting + conservative claims tied to demonstrable data quality.
Critique: This is an unusually detailed and disciplined revision that directly addresses common weaknesses in burst-based inference. The engineering plan is strong: the minimal single-zone transfer model, explicit Green’s-function delay kernel, rise-time preservation prior, and identifiability forecasting together constitute a technically executable and testable framework. Logical consistency is high; the causal chain from burst photons through a marginally optically thin reprocessing layer to observable hardness and lag signatures is physically sound and quantitatively constrained. The proposal is appropriately conservative about EOS claims and correctly reframes the scientific payoff as systematic-bias correction rather than precision M/R inference. Minor weaknesses remain: (i) the assumed shell geometry and effective step-length prescription, while justified as minimal, may still bias inferred r if the true medium is strongly anisotropic (e.g., equatorial wind), and this risk is only partially explored; (ii) the feasibility of measuring sub-ms lags in burst rises under realistic NICER deadtime/background conditions could be stressed more quantitatively; and (iii) the ionization-kinetics treatment relies on precomputed grids whose validity under extreme, rapidly varying burst spectra may need validation. These are limitations of scope rather than conceptual flaws.

Hypothesis: Superheavy nuclides (Z≥104) synthesized in a subset of neutron-star-merger ejecta produce a measurable, falsifiable distortion in late-time kilonova heating that arises from transport—not from the instantaneous-local-thermalization approximation—because spontaneous-fission fragments inject energy in a high-dE/dx, high-rigidity charged-particle channel whose deposition depth and time-delay depend differently on expansion, ionization state, and magnetic trapping than the beta/gamma channels that dominate actinide-only scenarios. The key claim is not that nuclear uncertainties are bypassed, but that (i) for any physically allowed superheavy source term consistent with broad priors on half-lives/branching and fission fragment spectra, the mapping from ‘injected decay power’ to ‘deposited heat’ is constrained by first-principles charged-particle slowing-down and pitch-angle scattering in expanding, partially ionized plasma, yielding a restricted family of deposition kernels; and (ii) this family produces a distinctive, testable pattern in multi-band light curves and nebular-phase spectra: a late-time color/bolometric evolution that requires simultaneously (a) enhanced charged-particle deposition relative to gamma deposition and (b) a temporally non-local heat release (delayed deposition tail) that cannot be matched, after marginalization, by actinide-only decay plus standard uncertainties (opacity evolution, gamma escape, ejecta stratification) or by smooth central-engine injection. We will demonstrate identifiability via Bayesian model comparison on synthetic and real datasets, explicitly propagating superheavy nuclear-input uncertainty through a kernel-operator formalism coupled to multi-D radiative transfer without double counting.
Plan:
Step 1 — Ejecta ensemble (astrophysical state space, controlled):
1.1 Build a physically constrained ejecta ensemble using numerical-relativity-informed parameterizations: total dynamical+wind mass M_ej∈[10^-3,10^-1] M_sun, velocity field v(r,θ) with homologous expansion v∝r after t0≈10–100 s, and axisymmetric density ρ(r,θ,t)=ρ0(θ)(t/t0)^-3.
1.2 Enforce causality-respecting equations of state through priors on compactness and tidal deformability (consistent with GW170817-like constraints), but keep macroscopic ejecta parameters free in inference to avoid over-conditioning.
1.3 Generate thermodynamic trajectories (entropy s, electron fraction Ye, expansion timescale τ) using a low-dimensional surrogate that spans: (A) lanthanide-poor, (B) lanthanide-rich, and (C) low-entropy, very neutron-rich channels favorable to superheavy formation. Each trajectory set produces an abundance “source-term family” rather than a single yield.

Step 2 — Kernel formalism (operator definition + governing equations):
2.1 Define the decay injection field for channel c∈{α, β±e, γ, fission fragments}:
Q_c(x,t,E,Ω)=∑_i n_i(x,t) λ_i b_{i,c} S_{i,c}(E,Ω),
where n_i is number density of nuclide i, λ_i its decay constant, b_{i,c} branching ratio into channel c, and S_{i,c} the normalized emission spectrum.
2.2 Define the deposition operator K acting on Q to yield volumetric heat deposition:
\dot{q}_dep(x,t)=∑_c \int d^3x' \int dt' \int dE \int dΩ\; K_c(x,t; x',t',E,Ω)\, Q_c(x',t',E,Ω).
K_c is a Green’s-function kernel encoding transport, energy loss, and escape in an expanding medium.
2.3 Transport approximations by channel (chosen to be accurate at late times t≳0.5 d when non-locality matters):
• γ-rays: grey/energy-dependent Monte Carlo or deterministic ray tracing in homologous expansion with absorption+Compton effective opacity κ_γ(E) (including Klein–Nishina), yielding an escape probability P_esc,γ(t;E,θ). Deposit via Compton electrons locally where interactions occur.
• β-electrons/α: continuous slowing down with pitch-angle scattering; treat with a 1D-in-radius Fokker–Planck (or Monte Carlo) in momentum space including adiabatic losses in expansion.
• Fission fragments: treat as heavy ions with initial kinetic-energy distribution (two-hump TKE with prior), charge state Z_eff(v,ne,T), and stopping dominated by Coulomb collisions with free electrons + bound-electron corrections. Use a CSDA+straggling correction to compute stopping length ℓ_ff(E,t) in a plasma with evolving ionization.
2.4 Plasma state and ionization closure:
Compute electron density ne(x,t) from Saha or collisional-radiative steady-state using local temperature from radiative transfer iterations; where non-LTE is expected (nebular phase), adopt an ionization parameterization ne=χ_e ρ/(μ_e m_p) with χ_e(t,θ) inferred with priors informed by lanthanide recombination physics. Stopping powers use ne and Coulomb logarithm lnΛ(T,ne).
2.5 Magnetic-field trapping:
Include an effective pitch-angle scattering mean free path λ_mfp = η r_L, with r_L=p/(Z_eff e B). Parameterize comoving B(t)=B0 (t/t0)^-2 (flux freezing) with prior B0∈[10^3,10^6] G at t0=10 s (broad, covering weak to strong trapping). This modifies the charged-particle kernel by reducing radial streaming and increasing residence time; implement via diffusion coefficient D≈(1/3) v λ_mfp and solve a diffusion-loss equation in the comoving frame.
2.6 Numerical scheme and coupling without double counting:
Iterate radiative transfer and deposition in operator-splitting:
(a) Given T, ρ, composition → compute opacities and plasma ionization.
(b) Evaluate deposition kernel K_c and compute \dot{q}_dep(x,t).
(c) Feed \dot{q}_dep as the sole radioactive/decay heat source into multi-D radiative transfer (e.g., Monte Carlo packets or moment-based solver). Energy conservation enforced by tracking injected decay energy minus escaped energy (γ and, if allowed, charged-particle escape) equals integrated deposition + adiabatic losses; verify by global budget checks per timestep.

Step 3 — Superheavy nuclear-input uncertainty model (priors + propagation):
3.1 Abundance parameterization (explicitly not “bypassed”):
Represent superheavy contribution by a parametric mass fraction X_SH at reference time t_ref=7.5 h (motivated by Asset 2), with X_SH prior log-uniform over [10^-6, 3×10^-2]. Allow the rest of heavy species to follow an actinide-rich baseline abundance vector from a standard r-process network, but marginalize over actinide production via an “actinide boost” parameter A_act.
3.2 Decay-chain and fission priors:
For an effective superheavy ensemble, define hyperparameters:
• half-life scale τ_SH (log-uniform 10^3–10^7 s),
• spontaneous-fission branching b_sf (Beta prior favoring high b_sf but allowing low),
• mean total kinetic energy ⟨TKE⟩ (Normal prior 170±20 MeV),
• fragment charge/mass split parameter (symmetric vs asymmetric mixture weight),
• prompt γ fraction f_γ (uniform/weakly informative), and delayed β component amplitude.
These hyperparameters generate S_ff(E) and channel partitions feeding Q_c.
3.3 Fission recycling/yield degeneracy control:
Include a nuisance “recycling opacity/thermalization” parameter that captures secondary heating from fission daughters, but constrain it with nuclear-physics-informed bounds. This prevents falsely attributing generic extra heating to superheavy fragments.
3.4 Uncertainty propagation:
Draw joint samples of (X_SH, τ_SH, b_sf, ⟨TKE⟩, yield-shape params, B0, η, χ_e(t), ejecta structure) → compute K → generate light curves/spectra. Quantify which observables remain stable (low variance) across nuclear priors while differing between SH and actinide-only models.

Step 4 — Observables and identifiability (falsifiable tests):
4.1 Define the data vector:
• Multi-band photometry: L_b(t) in optical/NIR/MIR bands, with emphasis on t≳3–30 d where γ escape and charged-particle deposition diverge.
• Color evolution: e.g., (F200W–F444W) for JWST-like filters, plus optical–NIR colors where available.
• Bolometric reconstruction with uncertainty.
• If spectra exist: nebular-phase line blanketing/continuum slope constraints used as weak composition/temperature priors (not claiming unique line IDs for superheavies).
4.2 Synthetic-data retrieval experiment (mandatory):
Generate mock datasets from:
(A) actinide-only + standard thermalization,
(B) actinide-only + full transport kernel,
(C) superheavy+actinide with full kernel,
(D) actinide-only + alternative power source (magnetar-like smooth injection with L∝(1+t/t_sd)^-2) and dust/opacity evolution.
Adopt realistic cadence/SNR: nightly sampling days 0.5–10, then every 3–5 days to day 40; photometric precision 0.05–0.1 mag (ground+HST) and 0.02–0.05 mag (JWST).
4.3 Model comparison:
Use Bayesian evidence (nested sampling) to compute Bayes factors K=Z_SH/Z_noSH under full marginalization over ejecta parameters, opacity evolution (time-dependent lanthanide fraction proxy), γ opacity scaling, ionization, and magnetic trapping. Define detection criterion: ln K > 5 (strong evidence) and posterior mass on X_SH above a threshold.
4.4 Minimal detectable superheavy fraction:
From retrieval, report X_SH,min such that ≥90% of realizations achieve ln K>5 given the cadence/SNR above, as a function of (M_ej, v, κ(t), B0). This directly answers “minimum required mass fraction”.
4.5 Application to real events:
Validate on AT2017gfo and AT2023vfi/GRB230307A-like light curves (Asset 1 context): first show actinide-only models can fit early times; then test whether late-time data prefer transport-only corrections or require an SH component. Report posterior odds and whether X_SH is bounded or only upper-limited.

Step 5 — Robustness and degeneracy stress tests:
5.1 Opacity evolution: include κ(t,θ) parameterization tied to recombination and composition gradients; verify SH inference is not an artifact of κ(t) flexibility.
5.2 Freeze-out/non-LTE: include a nebular “inefficiency” parameter that reduces thermal coupling; test whether it mimics SH signatures.
5.3 Gamma escape: allow κ_γ scaling and non-grey effects; ensure SH preference is not simply reduced γ trapping.
5.4 Engine/dust: include alternative components (smooth central engine; dust extinction/emission) and compute Bayes factors with/without them.

Deliverables:
• A publicly documented kernel module implementing K_c with selectable MC/deterministic solvers and verified energy conservation.
• Posterior constraints (or upper limits) on X_SH and associated nuclear hyperparameters for benchmark kilonovae.
• A detectability map X_SH,min(M_ej,v,κ,B0,cadence/SNR) guiding future JWST/HST/ELT follow-up strategies.
Feasibility:
1) The proposal no longer claims to eliminate nuclear uncertainties; instead it separates (a) source-term uncertainty (yields, half-lives, branching, fragment spectra) from (b) transport physics that is comparatively well constrained. By casting deposition as an explicit operator K acting on an injection field Q, we can propagate nuclear priors transparently and identify which late-time observables are controlled mainly by transport (robust) versus by poorly known nuclear microphysics (non-robust).
2) The kernel is implementable with established methods: γ transport via standard Monte Carlo with effective interaction physics; charged-particle energy loss via CSDA/Fokker–Planck using stopping-power theory with explicit plasma/ionization inputs; magnetic trapping via a diffusion-loss formulation parameterized by B0 and η. These components are individually validated in adjacent contexts (cosmic-ray transport, SN γ deposition) and can be benchmarked against limiting analytic scalings (e.g., deposition fraction ∝ t^-2 for freely streaming γ in homologous expansion).
3) Identifiability is addressed head-on with falsifiable Bayesian model comparison under realistic degeneracies. The synthetic retrieval suite includes actinide-only transport, opacity evolution, γ escape, non-LTE inefficiencies, dust, and magnetar-like injection. The requirement is not a qualitative ‘mismatch’ but quantified evidence (Bayes factors) and a derived minimum detectable X_SH.
4) Empirical plausibility is anchored in the literature assets: (i) kilonovae with lanthanide-rich ejecta of order ~0.02 M_sun (Asset 1) provide the regime where late-time transport/escape effects are observable; (ii) nucleosynthesis studies indicate superheavy mass fractions can reach X_{Z≥104}~3×10^-2 at ~hours post-merger under favorable conditions (Asset 2), setting a physically motivated upper range for our priors; and (iii) reported late-time deviations from simple heating laws motivate testing transport-based deposition.
5) Even null results are publishable and decisive: if Bayes factors consistently disfavor SH contributions and yield only stringent upper limits on X_SH across events, this constrains r-process pathways and superheavy production in neutron-star mergers in a way that conventional instantaneous-thermalization light-curve fits cannot.
Critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and technically mature proposal. Its strongest aspect is the clear separation between nuclear-input uncertainty and transport physics via an explicit Green’s-function kernel formalism, which directly targets a known weakness in kilonova modeling (the instantaneous-local-thermalization approximation). The transport treatments for gamma-rays, beta/alpha particles, and fission fragments are physically well motivated and internally consistent, and the inclusion of magnetic trapping and evolving ionization is appropriate for late-time ejecta. Logical flow from hypothesis to falsifiable observables is strong, and the identifiability strategy using Bayesian evidence and synthetic retrievals is exemplary. Minor weaknesses lie in the breadth of the parameter space (ejecta, plasma, nuclear hyperparameters, magnetic fields), which may dilute constraining power in practice, and in the reliance on simplified ionization closures (χ_e parameterization) that could partially reintroduce degeneracies the proposal aims to break. These are execution risks rather than conceptual flaws.

Hypothesis:
Z-source low-mass X-ray binaries traverse discrete, branch-dependent thermodynamic regimes in the neutron-star boundary layer (BL) and immediately adjacent inner disk, and these regime changes deterministically control (i) the centroid frequencies and (ii) the quality factors (Q) of the dominant timing components through a small set of physically coupled quantities: BL scale height H, effective sound speed c_s, radiative diffusion time t_diff, and shear/viscous damping time t_visc. We hypothesize that across the Z track (HB→NB→FB) the BL transitions between (A) a radiation-pressure-supported, optically thick spreading layer with short t_diff and strong radiative damping (low Q) and (B) a thinner, higher-c_s, less radiatively damped layer (higher Q), and that each observed QPO family corresponds to a pre-registered eigenfamily of this BL+transition-layer system. 

To address reviewer concerns about degeneracy/mode misidentification, we refine the forward model to a ‘two-zone’ BL framework with explicit eigenfamilies and a strict mode-identification protocol: (1) a compressible BL/slab supports acoustic p-modes and a buoyancy-modified branch (g/p mixed) whose eigenfrequencies scale with c_s/H and whose Q is set by radiative diffusion (t_diff) plus turbulent viscosity (alpha_BL); (2) a narrow transition layer (TL) connecting BL to the inner disk supports a low-frequency corrugation/tilt mode whose restoring torque depends on radiation pressure and effective gravity g_eff. The key mechanistic claim is that X-ray colors constrain (tau_es, T_e, y, and the BL luminosity fraction f_BL), which in turn uniquely determine H, c_s, and t_diff (via radiative equilibrium and hydrostatic balance), thereby fixing both frequency and damping for each eigenfamily. 

Radio: rather than an asserted ‘charge-starvation’ criterion, we posit a minimal, testable magnetospheric circuit + opacity gate. The same BL regimes modulate the pair injection rate into the closed magnetosphere (through gamma-gamma pair production in the BL Comptonizing field) and the baryon/wind loading near the light cylinder (through radiation-driven outflow). Coherent GHz bursts can escape only when (i) the magnetospheric potential drop exceeds a pair-screening threshold (insufficient pair supply) AND (ii) the surrounding plasma satisfies explicit propagation constraints (free–free absorption, induced Compton scattering, and Raman/strong scattering limits).
